articles.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
articles.body:
Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
- Published
Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."
The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.
Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."
Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.
Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.
"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
Earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.
Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity".

articles.title: Trump can strike Iran again. He cannot bomb Hormuz open
articles.body:
A navy can control water. It can’t make a merchant captain sail through it. Warships stop missiles, sure, but no admiral can promise a shipping company that its crew, its cargo and its insurance cover will all survive the next voyage. That gap is the real problem in the US-Iran war, and airstrikes alone won’t close it.
Look at what happened this month. Kpler data shows nearly 20.8 million barrels of oil passed through the strait on 8th October, but only 2.9 million on 11th October. A single day proves little, and Washington disputes independent tracking of the strait anyway. CENTCOM says about 97 percent of ships seeking to transit have done so without being hit. Still, the drop shows how fast a recovery falls apart once crews start to wonder whether passage could be fatal. AFP counted 23 attacks in the first two weeks of October, including six on a single day, the most since the war began, and the IMO says 24 seafarers have died in the area since February. On Saturday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said two loaded tankers caught fire after hitting mines, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.
President Donald Trump has said the US will not strike Iran before the 3rd November midterms, while insisting the blockade stays in force. Planners are reportedly readying options, including a massive ordnance air blast bomb, should he give the order. The diplomatic track is not dead, but it is stuck. Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the strait last month and now speaks of “productive discussions.” On Sunday, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the offer is still on the table: if Washington accepts Tehran’s conditions, the strait would open within six days and talks would resume on the seventh. Tehran hasn’t paused in the meantime. Reuters reported that Iran has changed how it picks its targets, and UK maritime authorities have logged attack after attack on tankers and container ships this month. The election may delay the next American bombing run. It does nothing about the bill the world is already paying.
Asia pays the most. Before the war, US Energy Information Administration data showed that 89 percent of the crude oil and condensate passing through Hormuz in the first half of 2025 was bound for Asian markets. China, India, Japan and South Korea took nearly three-quarters of it. The strait also carried over a fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas.
So when traffic stutters, the damage goes well beyond the oil price. Freight and insurance get dearer, and that lifts the cost of every barrel on arrival. Diesel runs short, which hurts trucking, farming and factories. Gas supplies lurch around, and anyone trying to plan electricity output is left guessing. The International Energy Agency’s October oil market report warned that renewed attacks were threatening the recovery in Gulf exports and that tight diesel markets were already cutting into incomes. And Reuters reported last month that marine fuel in Singapore was still more than 60 percent above prewar prices.
Gulf producers aren’t winning here either. The World Bank forecast this month that GCC economies will shrink by an average of 4.3 percent in 2026, with Qatar down 20.9 percent and Kuwait down 14.6 percent. Its rebound scenario for 2027 assumes the conflict eases by the end of this year, which is a big assumption. If it slips, the numbers get worse. Even Saudi Arabia’s workaround is under strain. Houthi attacks more than halved flows through Bab al-Mandeb in September, pushing Saudi crude back toward Hormuz, where it made up 43 percent of the strait’s oil traffic. Buyers and sellers are both being squeezed, and the Gulf partners Washington says it is defending are paying a good part of the cost.
The usual debate asks what options Trump has left. Keep the blockade and escort ships? Resume strikes? Take Kharg Island? Think about a wider ground war? That’s a list of tools, and a list of tools isn’t a strategy. The real question is whether any of them produces a waterway that commercial operators actually treat as open.
Naval escorts are the mildest option, and they do real work. They deter attacks and keep vital cargo moving. But Iran doesn’t have to beat the US Navy. A few surviving drones, missiles, small boats or mines will do, because they turn every voyage into a gamble. Guarding individual crossings for years isn’t the same as getting normal trade back.
READ: Iran’s IRGC Navy threatens to sink US warships approaching Strait of Hormuz
New air and missile strikes could wreck launch sites, command centres and coastal batteries, and things might go quiet for a while. They might also push Tehran to scatter what weapons it has left and hit softer targets around the Gulf. A Reuters investigation counted at least 135 strikes by Iran and allied forces on 84 infrastructure sites in seven Gulf countries since the war began in February. American force isn’t useless. But Iran can answer damage at home by causing trouble across a much wider regional economy.
Then there’s Kharg Island, which handles roughly 90% of Iran’s oil exports. It looks like a tempting prize, a possible bargaining chip. Yet the island sits only about 16 miles off Iran’s coast, well within reach of attack from the mainland. Take the island and you’ve signed up to defend and supply it, and that’s where the trouble starts. A full invasion would be a burden far out of proportion to the goal of keeping ships safe.
Escalation has a cost elsewhere, too. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates that replacing the Tomahawk missiles used in this war could take until late 2030. It doesn’t claim Washington is short of weapons for the Iranian fight. The concern is quieter: every high-end munition fired now is one that won’t be there in a Western Pacific crisis. A decision made in the Gulf ends up with a price tag in Asia.
I don’t think any of this means the United States should live with Iranian coercion of shipping. Attacks on civilian vessels have to stop. Seafarers aren’t bargaining chips. Washington and its partners have good reasons to protect navigation and keep up deterrence. But deterrence with no political way out turns into an expensive habit of managing danger without ever ending it.
So what would work? Something small and checkable, to begin with. Attacks on commercial ships would stop at once, and passage would be monitored and open to all vessels equally. Gulf states, shipowners and the relevant international maritime bodies would agree on how to report incidents and keep ships out of each other’s way. The blockade would ease in stages, each step by one side matched by a step from the other and tied to proof that commitments are being kept. Qatari-mediated exchanges show how far apart Washington and Tehran still are, which is exactly why verification and sequencing matter so much. Nuclear questions and wider regional disputes will still need negotiating. Merchant shipping shouldn’t have to wait for them.
Such a deal wouldn’t hand Iran a veto over Hormuz. It would test Tehran’s behaviour while leaving room to respond if attacks start again. And it wouldn’t guarantee peace. What it would offer is something another bombing campaign can’t: a way to tell whether the strait is getting safe enough for ordinary business to come back.
Asia and the Gulf shouldn’t sit and hope. China, India, Japan and South Korea deal with Washington and Tehran in very different ways, yet they share the same stake with the Gulf states that sit on the other side of the strait. They can press both sides in public for transit rules that can be checked, help with monitoring and incident reporting, and make clear to insurers and shipowners that the lanes will be trusted again only once the attacks end. The countries that take most of the strait’s cargo, and those that ship it, have the strongest claim to a say in how it reopens.
Trump can still order more strikes. He can turn up the pressure, grab territory or declare another tactical win. The harder test is whether he can turn military leverage into a lasting opening of the world’s most sensitive energy corridor. For Asia and the Gulf, that’s the difference between one more show of American firepower and a return to economic security.
Hormuz can’t be bombed back to normal. It has to be made safe enough for the world to trust again.

articles.title: Houthi missile strike kills 53 Yemeni soldiers, wounds 200 as Saudi Arabia cancels major summit
articles.body:
At least 53 Yemeni soldiers were killed and 200 others wounded Monday when Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles at a military training camp in southern Yemen, in one of the deadliest attacks since fighting intensified earlier this year, Yemeni military officials said. The strike came as Saudi Arabia canceled a major international investment conference following repeated Houthi attacks on its territory.
The missiles struck a camp in Shabwa province operated by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. According to a Yemeni military official, the attack occurred as newly recruited soldiers were lining up for a training session. The provincial government warned that the death toll could rise as authorities assessed the casualties.
The Shabwa authorities condemned the strike as a major escalation, saying it had targeted recruits undergoing training and preparation. They called on Yemen's presidential leadership and the Saudi-led coalition to accelerate the deployment of air defense and early warning systems to protect the province against further attacks.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, promised a "firm response," accusing the Houthis of resorting to terrorist attacks when facing military pressure. The rebels acknowledged carrying out the strike, claiming that the camp was operated by Saudi officers and that some had been killed. They provided no evidence to support that assertion, and Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The attack marks another escalation in Yemen's civil war, which has intensified since the broader conflict involving Iran began in February. The renewed fighting shattered a ceasefire established in 2022 that had largely halted major hostilities between the Houthis and government forces.
The Houthis, who control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north, have expanded their military operations in recent weeks, targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities while also capturing territory along the Red Sea coast near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
On Monday, the rebels claimed to have conducted six additional attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting oil facilities, military installations and Riyadh's international airport. They did not specify when the operations occurred. Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued danger alerts, although there were no immediate reports of casualties or damage from those latest claims.
The continuing attacks have begun disrupting major economic events in the kingdom. Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it was canceling an international investment conference scheduled for the following week, which had been expected to attract senior executives from Wall Street and other international financial institutions. The decision underscored the growing consequences of the Houthi campaign for Saudi Arabia's economy and international business activities.
The latest escalation follows a series of deadly incidents inside Yemen. On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry accused Saudi-led forces of carrying out an airstrike in the rebel-held northern province of Saada that killed at least nine people, including five children and two women. The rebels said additional strikes over the weekend had left more than 30 people dead or wounded. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to those allegations.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large areas of northern Yemen. Riyadh has long viewed the movement's military capabilities and its ties to Iran as a threat to its security. According to U.N. experts, Iran and allied groups in Lebanon and Iraq have provided the Houthis with military expertise, training and advanced weapons, although Tehran denies supplying arms to the rebels.
The conflict has taken on renewed strategic importance as Houthi forces advance near Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major offensive aimed at removing the rebels from recently captured territory along the coast.
Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department renewed its demand Monday for the release of more than 20 Yemeni employees of the American Embassy in Sanaa, marking five years since their detention by the Houthis. The embassy suspended operations in 2015, but local employees continued providing security and maintenance services. Washington called for their immediate and unconditional release.

articles.title: US issues security alerts for Middle East, Yemen war rages
articles.body:
US embassies in the West Asian region issued security warnings to US citizens in the region, citing potential threats from Iran and Yemen’s Houthis on US citizens and interests
War in Yemen continues with tit-for-tat strikes between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he hopes the Islamic world can resolve its challenges and differences at an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation meeting in Baghdad, Iraq, and conducted various meetings with other country reps
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires.
And so we continue our live coverage...
Govt staff in Saudi capital told to work from home
Government agencies in Saudi capital Riyadh have told employees to work from home starting Monday, one worker and two consultants told AFP, as the city comes under repeated attack from Yemen's Houthis.
The Kingdom Centre, a 99?storey tower in downtown Riyadh that houses the regional office of the International Monetary Fund, has also requested workers in its offices to stay away until further notice.
On Sunday evening, an employee working for a government agency in Riyadh received a message saying "it has been decided to implement remote work from Monday to Thursday this week".
"We ask everyone to continue their activities as normal," it added.
Death toll of Houthi attack on Yemen govt camp over 50
More than 50 people were killed and over 200 wounded when Yemen's Houthis hit a military camp in energy-rich Shabwa province with ballistic missiles, officials and military sources said on Monday.
It marked the deadliest attack in weeks as fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised, Saudi-supported government escalates after the collapse of a years-long truce.
"More than 53 recruits" were killed and over 200 injured, all new members of the internal security forces who were undergoing training, Shabwa authorities said in a statement.
Three ballistic missiles struck al-Alam camp in Shabwa, two military sources said. Majed al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the Yemeni armed forces, described it as a training centre for security and police recruits.
Egypt delays Saudi military support vote until 26 October
An Egyptian parliamentary vote on whether to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia, should the kingdom request support, has been postponed until 26 October.
The vote had been scheduled to take place this week.

Israel Katz boasts about wiping over 60 Lebanese villages

Lebanese President Aoun says Israel has not adhered to the framework agreement signed in June, adding “daily violations” in southern Lebanon “do not help the Lebanese state” to implement its side of the treaty.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has unveiled a security doctrine advocating pre-emptive military strikes and buffer zones along Israel's borders, despite the collapse of his previous security strategy during the 7 October 2023 attack, while displaying maps of supposed regional alliances just days before Israeli elections.
The three-page document, titled "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Security Concept", was published on the Israeli government's website on Sunday and outlines the country's alleged principal security threats and 10 central principles guiding its military strategy.
Russia's foreign minister has arrived in Tehran for his first visit since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported on Monday, as Moscow seeks to play a mediating role.
Arriving from Bahrain, Sergei Lavrov was scheduled to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
His visit comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart earlier this month that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Iran will respond forcefully to new US attacks: official
An adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said Iran will respond forcefully to any renewed US attack.
Conservative politician Mohammad Mokhber said Iran would strike “nine countries” if Iranian bases or “petrochemical” facilities were struck again, not directly naming the nine.
“If they want to hit a base, we have to hit the bases of nine countries,” he said Monday in recorded comments posted by Tasnim, a semiofficial news agency close with the Revolutionary Guard.
Houthi rebels strike a government military camp in south
UN rights experts on Monday called on Israel to protect Palestinian farmers in the West Bank as settler attacks worsen with the annual olive harvest.
"Palestinian farmers must be protected and able to access their land safely. Yet, year after year, the violence, destruction and restrictions intensify," the experts said in a statement.
"The olive harvest should be a time when farmers can enjoy, in safety and dignity, the food and livelihoods their nature and land provide, not another season of fear, loss, violence and destruction."
The experts urged Israel to ensure that is forces protect Palestinian farmers from settler attacks and refrain from interference with their access to land. They also urged the international community to "exercise maximum pressure to protect Palestinian civilians".
Israeli violence on Palestinians is surging in the territory ahead of Israel's bitterly fought October 27 elections. The vote coincides with Palestinians' annual olive harvest which has been disrupted by Israeli settlers as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeks to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base.
Govt operations continue against Houthis in Bab al-Mandeb
Sources in Bab al-Mandab told The New Arab that military operations by the internationally recognised government are continuing against the Houthis.
The sources also said that government forces are fighting two battles, the first to "clear" the Houthis and their vehicles, and the second to clear the lands of mines in very large numbers.
Israel kills 5 in Gaza over past 24 hours: health ministry
According to the Palestinian ministry of health in Gaza, since the alleged ceasefire in October 2024, Israel killed 1,522 Palestinians, wounded 5,421 and 839 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.
Over the past 24 hours, Israel killed five Palestinians and wounded 22, the ministry reported.
"In each of the previous wars, you [referring to the United States and Israel] entered battle with the slogan of overthrowing the Islamic Republic, dismembering and destroying Iran; yet today you are the ones being destroyed and overthrown while a powerful Iran still stands firm," Iran's chief of staff of the armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi said, in remarks carried by state-run media.
The chief of staff said "the next miscalculation against Iran" will be met with more severe responses than before.
Leaders of the Palestinian community still within the 1948 territories and hold Israeli citizenship are urging people in the community to vote in big numbers in next week's election as they seek to unseat fundamentalist Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and topple the most fanatical right-wing government in the country's history.
High turnout by the 21% 1948 Palestinian community could nudge Israel's complex coalition arithmetic in favour of an anti-Netanyahu bloc led by a former military chief, Gadi Eisenkot.
Qatar will soon announce local defence production hub
Qatar will soon announce a defence production hub, the minister of state for defence affairs told the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday.
Against the background of the Middle East conflict, which has drawn Iranian attacks on the energy-rich Gulf countries, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said: "We are partnering with a regional partner, in addition to other partners such as the United States, the United Kingdom, France, to make sure either we do local protection or we are investing in some of these companies."
WFP ending aid for half million in Gaza due to no funds
The UN's World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, while warning that needs remained acute.
"As of this month, we're now cutting half a million people from the number of people that we're assisting," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP.
The reductions bring down to 1.1 million people—still roughly half of war-battered Gaza's population—the number of Palestinians receiving WFP aid either in food or cash assistance.
US President Donald Trump on Sunday offered his "complete and total" endorsement of ICC fugitive Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the country's 27 October elections.
"Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel. BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 people in the occupied West Bank after Israeli settler attacks on an US photographer for The Washington Post and a French mayor.
The police said that they raided several locations across the occupied West Bank and also seized cars and potential evidence related to the attacks, which have stepped up as Israeli settlers disrupt Palestinians' annual olive harvest.
"Following the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians, an arrest operation was conducted before dawn," said Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's occupied West Bank commander.
"Suspects were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the violent incidents, violating a military commander's order concerning a closed military zone, and illegal construction," he said.
The attacks come after global outrage over mounting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
Lebanon military delegation to try to halt Israeli attacks
A Lebanese military delegation will present Beirut's demands for an end to Israeli attacks in Lebanon at a trilateral meeting in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October, the Lebanese presidency said in a post on X on Saturday.
Under a deal reached through US-brokered Israel-Lebanon talks, Beirut vowed to disarm Hezbollah, which would in turn lead to Israeli troops gradually withdrawing from Lebanon. But Israel continues to strike the south of the country.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will visit Tehran today, Monday, for consultations with Iranian officials and aims to follow up on the implementation of bilateral agreements, Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement.
Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: IRGC
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway.
Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil.
The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting.
"An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room," Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying.
The tanker was travelling in the strait's "unauthorized southern route" and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said.
It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines.

articles.title: Houthi ballistic missile strike kills at least 53 Yemen govt troops
articles.body:
Houthi rebels killed at least 53 Yemeni government soldiers in a ballistic missile strike on a military camp Monday, one of the deadliest attacks since fighting surged this summer, military officials said.
The attack wounded an additional 200 recruits at the military camp in the southern province of Shabwa, the provincial government there said. The rebels acknowledged targeting the camp.
The fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces is a widening front in the Iran war that began in February. The escalation shattered a 2022 cease-fire deal that largely stopped fighting in Yemen’s civil war.
The Houthis have put their growing military capabilities on display on multiple fronts in recent weeks, repeatedly striking Saudi Arabia’s main international airport hundreds of kilometers away and seizing territory inside Yemen near a key shipping chokepoint.
Iran and its allies in Lebanon and Iraq provide expertise, training and sophisticated weapons to the Houthis, according to U.N. and other experts. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would violate a U.N. embargo.
The provincial government in Shabwa said in a statement that the death toll is preliminary and may rise. It said the recruits were receiving training to be part of internal security forces.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the statement said.
It called on Yemen’s president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa’s capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
On Sunday, an airstrike blamed on Saudi-led forces killed at least nine people in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said. Five children and two women were killed in the attack, one of several that killed or wounded more than 30 people over the weekend, according to the rebels.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis, a Shiite religious and political movement rooted in northern Yemen, are increasingly attacking Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The Sunni kingdom, which has long feared the emergence of a well-armed ally of Shiite Iran on its border, joined the war in 2015 after the rebels seized much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
The rebels have been targeting Saudi airports and oil and military facilities. The headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco has been struck as well in a blow to the world’s top oil exporter.
The rebels also recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Saudi-led coalition this month launched a major military offensive to dislodge the rebels from that strategic perch and retake the territory.

articles.title: Why Russia's war on Ukraine's data centers could backfire on Moscow
articles.body:
Why Russia's war on Ukraine's data centers could backfire on Moscow
People use their mobile phones as they walk past the Moscow City business center in Moscow, Russia, on April 15, 2026. (Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images)
Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers could backfire, experts have told the Kyiv Independent, as Kyiv's retaliatory attacks have exposed vulnerabilities in how Moscow has organized IT infrastructure.
On Sept. 23, a Russian attack damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions. The attack also affected cloud service Fex.net and disrupted internet access for around 100,000 households in Kyiv. Since then, Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine's digital infrastructure.
Moscow is expanding its targets to find new ways to pressure Ukraine as its battlefield offensives in 2026 have failed to achieve their objectives, Tetiana Trach, a Russia researcher at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), told the Kyiv Independent. The strikes on data centers fit into Russia's broader campaign to damage Ukraine's economy and make civilian life harder.
Ukraine, which has increasingly used long-range strikes to weaken Russia's ability to sustain the war, retaliated. Between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18, Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK.
But while Ukraine suffers from daily Russian drone and missile barrages, Russia faces a different problem. Serhiy Petrenko, former Yandex Ukraine head, estimated that around 80% of Russia's data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region — within reach of Ukrainian long-range drones.
Russia's centralized digital infrastructure leaves Moscow facing two challenges: inflicting comparable damage on Ukraine and protecting its own data centers from further strikes. Experts say neither will be easy.
"Russian data centers appear more vulnerable than Ukrainian ones. Russia appears willing to accept this risk," Trach said.
The Russian pro-war milblogger 'Art Jockey' said that attacks on data centers had previously been treated as an informal red line between the two countries, and that Moscow's decision to target Ukrainian facilities had opened the door to retaliation.
"With no end in sight to the war he started nearly five years ago, Putin opted for another round of escalation," they wrote. "It's not that no one had thought of attacking data centers before. Putin simply decided to make the first move now, effectively removing the restraints on Ukraine as well."
read also
Can Russia knock Ukraine offline?
Russia's war against Ukraine in 2026 can be seen as a contest between two strategies of long-range attacks, with both sides seeking to increase pressure beyond the battlefield, a July analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) concluded. The recent strikes on data centers fit that pattern.
Following a meeting with military leaders on Sept. 25, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the Ukrainian government had decided to strengthen the protection of data centers and other critical communications infrastructure.
Despite the recent damage, knocking out internet access across Ukraine would be extremely difficult, Anatolii Frolenkov, a representative of the 1-IX internet exchange point, told the Kyiv Independent in September.
"Russian strikes would have to be continuous and happen at a hundred different sites to be effective."
"The internet will not disappear completely," Frolenkov said. "There will be outages, there will be problems. It won't work as smoothly or as quickly, things may glitch, and operators may go down for a couple of hours because the infrastructure is being physically destroyed."
Samuel Bendett, an expert on Russian military technology at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) and the Center for Naval Analyses (CNA), told the Kyiv Independent that "Russian strikes would have to be continuous and happen at a hundred different sites to be effective."
Trach agreed that Russia could continue causing temporary internet outages in Ukraine but said a nationwide shutdown was unlikely given the country's decentralized infrastructure.
Ukraine strikes back
On Oct. 8, outages occurred in many segments of the Russian internet at about 4 p.m. local time, especially in Moscow and St. Petersburg, after Ukraine struck a Yandex data center, the Moscow Times said. Several banking services, Google, RuTube, the website of the Russian Railways, and many retail websites were unreachable.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky commented on the attack. "We always respond in kind."
Subsequent Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers in October disrupted payments, banking, and online services in Russia, while parts of the infrastructure were still recovering more than a week later.
"This is the first serious problem with potentially major consequences for Russia's financial system, and the campaign against data centers has only been going on for a few days," the milblogger Art Jockey said on Oct. 12.
He warned that if Ukraine disabled the main services of Sberbank, Russia's largest lender, it could trigger panic among depositors and mass withdrawals.
Two days later, Ukrainian drones struck a Sberbank data center under construction in Balakovo. The bank confirmed the attack but said its services were operating normally.
"You didn't think it would end with Yandex, did you?" Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said the same day on social media platform Threads.
On Oct. 18, VK confirmed an attack on its data center in Leningrad Oblast but said its services remained operational. Users, however, reported disruptions across the social network and its affiliated platforms, according to Downdetector, a service that tracks online outages.
read also
Consequences for Russia
The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology.
"The Russians, I think, didn't think it would get that far, that fast."
"Yandex and other data centers that were hit are going to set Russian AI development back significantly," Bendett said.
Yandex and Sberbank are both major players in Russia's AI development, while the state plays a central role in the sector. Russia also recently announced plans to share drone attack data with developers to train neural networks and algorithms, according to Bendett.
While Russia's military AI programs have traditionally operated separately from commercial developers, they still depend on some of the same computing resources, advanced chips, and civilian specialists. Western sanctions also complicate replacing damaged equipment.
"The dependence could be quite substantial. And if civilian specialists are raising the alarm about these attacks, then Russian military AI could be impacted," Bendett added.
Can Russia protect itself?
"Is there any hope for air defenses?" a Art Jockey asked, answering his own question with "there isn't much hope."
"Sooner or later, if Ukraine decides to strike this facility, its drones will get through — if not on the first attempt, then on the second or third," he said.
On Oct. 12, Russian Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said his ministry was discussing data center protection with the Defense Ministry, according to Russian news agency Interfax.
Two days later, President Vladimir Putin convened senior officials for a cybersecurity meeting, although the Kremlin denied any connection to Ukrainian drone strikes.
Besides government ministers and top security officials, the meeting included Sberbank chief executive Herman Gref and central bank governor Elvira Nabiullina, according to Reuters.
On Oct. 16, Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed housing data centers inside depleted open-pit mines and quarries, given their natural protection from aerial bombardment.
"The Russians, I think, didn't think it would get that far, that fast," Bendett said.
"Now they're scrambling for solutions, like putting data centers underground or farther away. But what's done is done."

articles.title: Russia Bombards Kyiv and Surrounding Region With Missiles and Drones, Killing Two and Injuring 14
articles.body:

Russia Bombards Kyiv and Surrounding Region With Missiles and Drones, Killing Two and Injuring 14
Russian forces launched a large-scale missile and drone attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on October 19, killing at least two people and injuring 14 others, including three children.
The attack involved ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hundreds of drones, damaging residential buildings, medical facilities, educational institutions, and transport infrastructure across the capital and Kyiv region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, one person was killed and eight others were injured in the capital, where damage was recorded in the Desnianskyi, Dniprovskyi, and Solomianskyi districts.
In the Desnianskyi district, the strikes damaged a private medical facility and a metro station. Authorities subsequently announced the temporary closure of the Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations on Kyiv’s left bank.
Debris from the attack damaged both the running and power rails near one of the stations, disrupting metro operations in the affected area.
In the Dniprovskyi district, falling debris damaged educational institutions and a sports facility, while additional debris landed on nonresidential premises.
Meanwhile, in the Solomianskyi district, a fire broke out inside a medical facility located on the third floor of a 25-story residential building. Emergency services extinguished the blaze, while the attack also damaged windows in nearby buildings and a shopping center.
The missile strikes also raised concerns about the lack of advance warning for residents. According to sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu, the ballistic missile attack on Kyiv once again occurred without any warning, a situation that has reportedly happened on previous occasions.
Beyond the capital, Russian strikes caused casualties and extensive damage in several communities across Kyiv region, particularly in Irpin, Bucha district.
According to Head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration Tymur Tkachenko, six people were injured in Irpin, including three children, while three others were reported missing. Deputy Mayor Oleksandr Pashchynskyi also confirmed that a woman had been killed in the attack.
In the wider Bucha district, the strikes damaged 11 private houses, six vehicles, an industrial facility, a warehouse, and an educational institution. Windows were also shattered in several apartment buildings.
In the Vyshhorod district, authorities reported damage to a private residence, five vehicles, and an infrastructure facility.
The overnight assault formed part of a broader Russian aerial attack involving multiple types of missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles launched from Russian territory and occupied Ukrainian regions.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from Russia’s Smolensk, Bryansk, and Kursk regions, as well as Iskander-K cruise missiles from the airspace over the Kursk region.
The attack also involved 269 drones, including Shahed-type attack UAVs, S-8000 Banderol drones, Gerbera drones, and Parodiya decoys. Of the total, 59 were jet-powered drones.
As of 9 a.m. on October 19, Ukrainian air defenses had intercepted or suppressed 247 aerial targets, including four Iskander-K cruise missiles and 243 drones of various types. Among the intercepted drones were 43 jet-powered UAVs, according to the Air Force’s preliminary assessment.
The latest attack comes amid renewed attention to Ukraine’s access to intelligence needed to detect incoming Russian missile strikes. On October 18, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that the United States had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine following a temporary suspension, restoring a key channel of military cooperation amid concerns over the availability of early warnings about Russian missile attacks.

articles.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver, says he does not want to drive Moscow from talks
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on 18 October that he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” He also wrote: “Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!”
Trump was referring to sanctions and tariffs under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he waived in an executive order on 16 October, days before the measures were due to take effect. The waiver suspends additional economic penalties intended to pressure Moscow over its war against Ukraine, while leaving earlier US sanctions in place. The decision came weeks before the 3 November midterms, in which Republicans are defending slim majorities in both chambers, and analysts said the penalties could have pushed up oil prices for Americans already paying more, largely because of the US-Israeli war with Iran, Reuters reported.
Trump says Zelenskyy could have made a better deal two years ago
A week before the waiver, Trump had announced a deal for Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets. The Treasury also issued a license, valid until 7 April 2027, permitting certain transactions in Russian-origin diesel.
In the Truth Social post, Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of targeting Russian diesel refineries, saying the strikes were “seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.” Kyiv had paused its refinery strikes for three days at Washington’s request after Trump declared an energy ceasefire on 11 October, which Russia never confirmed, then resumed them. Since then, Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy sector 76 times, Zelenskyy said on 18 October.
Kyiv gets no warning of the first of two Russian ballistic waves, hours after Zelenskyy said US alerts were back
Trump wrote that Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” and that he “could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now.”
“His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead,” Trump added.
He also said Russia was “doing very little, if anything, to help” Iran and that he wanted to keep it that way.
A day earlier, Trump said he had not made a final decision
On 17 October, Trump told reporters at Mar-a-Lago that he had not announced his final decision. “A lot of you don’t know what my decision is yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said, Reuters reported.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters before departing for Uzbekistan the same day.
Zelenskyy calls the waiver a pity as Republicans split
Zelenskyy called it a “pity” that Trump had waived sanctions under a law named for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who “really believed in Ukraine.” He said he hoped Trump would change his decisions, NBC News reported.
Discussing the diesel deal on NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelenskyy said US oil prices had risen because shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was blocked, not because of Ukraine.
A month before the diesel waiver, Trump’s envoys had already pitched Kyiv on Russian gas, NYT says
On 17 October, Zelenskyy told journalists that “the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me” and that it “definitely helps only the Russians.” His remarks appeared in Ukrainian on his official Telegram channel.
“Sanctions relief will continue. I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” Zelenskyy said.
On 19 October, Zelenskyy wrote that partners had again given no warning of Russia’s overnight ballistic attack and that blocking missiles for Ukraine’s air defense while Russia gets sanctions eased or postponed amounts to partners denying reality.
Republican Senator James Lankford defended Trump’s decision on NBC’s Meet the Press, saying the president was “choosing the American people first.”
Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom Trump has endorsed for a full term, said at a campaign stop on 17 October that she would “choose to keep the pressure on Russia.”
“I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” Darline Graham said.
She did not directly criticize Trump but said she would not have made that choice, Reuters reported.

articles.title: Egypt weighs sending troops to defend Saudi Arabia as Houthis warn of another Yemen disaster
articles.body:
Egypt's parliament continued deliberations Monday over whether to send military forces to Saudi Arabia to help Riyadh defend itself against attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, as the Iran-backed group warned Cairo against intervening and invoked the disastrous Egyptian military campaign in Yemen during the 1960s.
The discussions follow a request by Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi on Saturday to convene parliament and authorize military assistance to the Saudis. In a speech, el-Sissi declared his country's full support for defending the territory of its Gulf allies and pledged to take whatever steps Saudi Arabia requested to protect its security and sovereignty. The statement was seen as an unusual signal of Egypt's willingness to become involved in the conflict.
El-Sissi's initial declaration left the exact nature of the proposed assistance somewhat unclear. However, Egyptian lawmaker Mostafa Bakry offered more details in a statement Sunday, explaining that parliament would discuss the president's decision, in his capacity as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, to send military forces to Saudi Arabia on a defensive mission.
Bakry said Egypt's National Defense Council, chaired by el-Sissi, had already approved the proposed deployment and its assigned mission before parliamentary deliberations began. The council's public statement pledged support for Saudi Arabia but did not specify the deployment of troops.
"Egypt has never abandoned its pan-Arab role or its responsibility to safeguard Arab national security," Bakry said. "For us, Saudi Arabia is an integral part of Egypt's own national security, and any threat to its security and stability is also a threat to us."
The parliamentary discussions were extended after additional lawmakers requested an opportunity to speak. Bakry subsequently indicated that a vote could take place Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Lebanon's Al-Akhbar newspaper, which is affiliated with Hezbollah and the Iranian-led axis, claimed Monday that Egypt already has military personnel in Saudi Arabia, although their presence has not been publicly acknowledged.
"Cairo is preparing to officially send forces to the kingdom after weeks of undeclared military presence, while refusing to participate in operations inside Yemen," the newspaper reported.
According to Al-Akhbar, several Egyptian military personnel arrived in Saudi Arabia weeks ago. Egyptian military sources cited by the newspaper claimed that the decision to publicly announce the move and seek parliamentary approval was prompted by rapid developments on the ground requiring additional forces, alongside consideration of supplying Riyadh with defensive weapons.
The sources said the priority in coordination with Saudi Arabia was deploying air defense batteries and providing logistical support to secure several vital facilities in the kingdom.
According to the report, the Egyptian forces would undertake defensive missions, including protecting civilians and helping reduce damage from surprise attacks. The sources insisted that Egyptian troops were not expected to participate in offensive operations inside Yemen and claimed that additional forces could begin arriving in Saudi Arabia within days.
Saudi Arabia's request for Egyptian assistance comes after weeks of significant casualties and damage caused by Houthi missile and drone attacks. The rebels say the attacks are retaliation for the Saudi air blockade of Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen and for military operations against them by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized government, which Riyadh supports.
The deadliest recent attack on Saudi Arabia occurred when a Houthi missile struck Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and injuring more than 300.
The continuing attacks are also damaging Saudi Arabia's economy and threatening Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030, an ambitious program aimed at diversifying the kingdom's economy and reducing its dependence on traditional sources of revenue.
Egypt's parliamentary discussions come just over a month after Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 and met with el-Sissi.
Following that meeting, the Egyptian presidency said the two leaders had reaffirmed their commitment to ensuring freedom of navigation and maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, where the Houthis have recently tightened their control over nearby areas and shipping routes.
El-Sissi stressed Egypt's opposition to any attack targeting Saudi Arabia or threatening freedom of navigation along international shipping routes. The statement said both leaders agreed that the current circumstances required greater solidarity and coordination between their countries.
Egypt is among the countries most vulnerable to security developments around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Although the Houthis are currently concentrating their attacks on Saudi Arabia, Egypt, farther north, depends heavily on revenue from the Suez Canal, which is reached through the strait and the Red Sea.
Any escalation in the area can therefore cause substantial economic damage to Cairo.
For that reason, although Egypt is generally reluctant to enter military alliances and prefers to maintain a neutral position as a regional mediator, it has a clear interest in ending the confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis as quickly as possible.
The Houthis, who are closely following developments in Egypt, have already begun issuing warnings to Cairo.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi political bureau, told Qatar's Al-Araby television that the Egyptian military carries bitter memories of its involvement in Yemen between 1962 and 1968, and said he could not imagine it repeating that experience.
Al-Bukhaiti was referring to the events following a military coup in Yemen in September 1962, when Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser decided to support the republicans fighting royalist forces and sent some of Egypt's most elite military units into the country.
Egypt paid a heavy price for that intervention. Over the course of the conflict, it deployed approximately 70,000 soldiers to defend the new government and became trapped in a prolonged war fought under difficult conditions, with mountainous terrain and few roads.
The campaign, which ultimately forced Egyptian troops to withdraw, is still sometimes referred to as "Egypt's Vietnam."
In his interview with Al-Araby, al-Bukhaiti also mocked Saudi Arabia's leadership, claiming that el-Sissi's remarks exposed the depth of the kingdom's humiliation.
The Saudi leadership, he said, had reached a point where it was begging other countries to defend and protect it, even though, in the Houthis' view, Saudi Arabia itself was the aggressor. "We do not expect Egypt to become involved in aggression against Yemen. Egypt is bigger than that," he said. He added that such an intervention would place Egypt in the same camp as the United States and Israel.
Meanwhile, Al-Akhbar reported Monday that Houthi intelligence was monitoring movements by foreign forces that had allegedly arrived in Jizan, in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border. According to the newspaper, the area has become a staging ground for planning attacks against Yemen.
The report claimed that Pakistani forces were also present, following a defense alliance recently signed by Pakistan and Turkey with Saudi Arabia. It further alleged that Ukrainian personnel had arrived in the area several days earlier aboard a military transport aircraft. Those reports have not been independently verified.
The Houthis have threatened to target foreign forces involved in military operations against them, raising the possibility that Egyptian, Pakistani or Ukrainian personnel could come under attack if they participate in the campaign.
Fighting inside Yemen is also continuing between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
On Monday, reports from Yemen described a major Houthi attack on the al-Alam military base in Shabwa province, allegedly carried out during a training exercise. Dozens of Yemeni government troops were reportedly killed or wounded.
Houthi missile and drone launches toward Saudi Arabia have also continued. Early Monday morning, an alert was issued in Jizan following reports of another launch.

articles.title: The US did not explain the Starlink restrictions and the lack of warning about Russia's strike: Zelenskyy revealed the details
articles.body:
The US did not explain the Starlink restrictions and the lack of warning about Russia's strike: Zelenskyy revealed the details
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine did not receive early warning of the first wave of Russia's ballistic attack. The US also did not explain the restrictions on Starlink and Starshield.
Ukraine did not receive early warning from its partners about the first wave of the overnight ballistic missile attack, and the U.S. side has still not explained the reasons for this. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this during a meeting with representatives of both parties and chambers of the U.S. Congress, reports UNN, citing the official Telegram channel of the head of state.
The Ukrainian leader also informed the partners about the consequences of Russia’s attack on the Kharkiv region, problems with the exchange of intelligence data, and restrictions on the operation of Starlink and Starshield on the front.
Details
During the conversation, Zelenskyy informed American lawmakers about Russia’s attack on the Kharkiv region using attack drones, which killed six people, including a woman and her child, who was slightly over a year old. The president also showed photographs from the scene of the tragedy depicting the aftermath of the shelling.
"I showed horrific photographs from the scene of the tragedy: a murdered child in a stroller… This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the reduction of pressure," Zelenskyy emphasized.
The parties paid particular attention to the exchange of intelligence and the operation of the American satellite communications services Starlink and Starshield, which are used by the Ukrainian military. According to Zelenskyy, during the latest massive attack, Ukraine did not receive timely warning about Russia’s use of ballistic missiles.
"Unfortunately, we did not receive early warning from our partners about the first wave of Russia’s ballistic missile attack last night. And we are still facing speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield services in various areas of the front," the president said.
He stressed that the American side had provided Ukraine with no explanations either for the lack of early warning about the missile attack or for the restrictions on the operation of satellite communications. At the same time, Zelenskyy noted that the Ukrainian and American teams would continue working to resolve all the issues raised during the meeting.
"Our teams will continue working on all the issues discussed today. I thank everyone who took part in the conversation for their strong support," the head of state concluded.
Recall
Earlier, Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed with representatives of a U.S. defense company the supply of missiles for Patriot and the repair of F-16s in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine Exposes Foreign-Made Components Behind Russia’s Anti-Jamming Tech Used in Missiles and Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Exposes Foreign-Made Components Behind Russia’s Anti-Jamming Tech Used in Missiles and Drones
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) has identified foreign-made components used in the production of Russia’s Kometa anti-jamming navigation modules, which are installed in Russian missiles, attack drones, and guided aerial bombs.
According to HUR from Ukraine’s military intelligence, the modules are designed to protect onboard navigation systems against electronic warfare interference, allowing Russian weapons to maintain navigation capabilities in contested environments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Kometa system uses controlled reception pattern antennas, which can suppress interference by adjusting the antenna’s reception pattern and applying signal-processing algorithms.
According to HUR, a standard Kometa module used in modern Russian missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and guided aerial bombs consists of two main components: an antenna array containing a specified number of patch antennas and a signal-processing module based on a programmable logic device.
The system’s resistance to electronic interference depends on the number and arrangement of its patch antennas, as well as the algorithms used to process incoming signals.
By combining signals received through multiple antennas, the module can determine the direction of incoming interference and reduce its impact on the navigation system.
Ukrainian intelligence reported that Russian forces are already widely deploying Kometa modules equipped with 16 patch antennas, while efforts are underway to establish serial production of more advanced 20-element antenna arrays.
HUR also identified the Russian company VNIIR-Progress as the developer and primary manufacturer of various Kometa modifications. The enterprise belongs to the ABS Electro group of companies, which Ukrainian intelligence linked to sanctioned Serbian pro-Russian politician Nenad Popović.
According to the intelligence agency, another company within the same group is responsible for procuring components needed to manufacture the navigation modules. The supply network includes Chinese distributors and sellers of microelectronics, as well as Russian intermediaries involved in obtaining foreign-made electronic components.
To fulfill orders from Russia’s defense industry, VNIIR-Progress uses both its own manufacturing facilities and the production capacities of other companies within the ABS Electro group. HUR also identified the principal customers for Kometa modules as Russian manufacturers of cruise and ballistic missiles, attack drones, guided aerial bombs, and glide munitions.
In a separate investigation published on October 14, The Insider reported that Chinese technology company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology was prepared to supply mesh communication modems to a Russian drone manufacturing facility despite being informed that the equipment was intended for military use.
The investigation found that the company was willing to deliver communication systems to a drone production facility in Alabuga, Russia, where the equipment could be used to support long-range drone attacks against Ukraine.

articles.title: Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine
articles.body:
Rubio says there was no US pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine
Ukraine relies on US intel provided through Starshield system to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia fires at its cities.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied any suspension of intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington has resumed providing critical intelligence to help Kyiv defend against Russian missile strikes.
“There has been no pause,” Rubio told reporters while on a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday. “What [Zelenskyy] should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war.”
Ukraine has relied on US intelligence through Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, to detect the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities.
Asked about a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the more than four-year Ukraine war, Rubio said: “There’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know whether it’s been finalised, but the president [Trump] has been clear. He’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end.”
The comments were made after Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning. Speaking to the NBC TV network’s Meet the Press programme on Sunday, Zelenskyy said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but was later “deblocked”.
“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”
Waiving sanctions on Russia
Zelenskyy also said other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russia that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine.
“If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course, we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand,” he said.
Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia while accusing Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He claimed that “Zelenskyy doesn’t care” about ending the conflict. “Frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Trump has temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing large quantities to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices.
The US president also reiterated his accusation that Ukraine was purposefully targeting Russian refineries to try to hurt Trump’s Republican Party in the November 3 midterm elections.
Polling has suggested Trump’s party is heading for a likely defeat in the elections as many voters are upset by fuel costs, which have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spoke with Meet the Press after it aired Zelenskyy’s interview, saying the Ukrainian president “presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win”.
“The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement,” he said.
Bessent slammed the claim that the US government was behind the slowing of the SpaceX satellite communications. “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” he said. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a Russian missile attack killed a woman and wounded several people in the capital, Kyiv, overnight, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Monday.
The attack also damaged a metro station, a medical facility, an educational institution and a nonresidential building, according to the State Emergency Service.

articles.title: Ukraine ‘received no early warning’ of Russian strikes
articles.body:
People look at damaged office center after a Russian missile attack in central Kyiv, Ukraine, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (AP Photo)
Ukraine did not receive an early warning from allies about incoming Russian ballistic strikes that targeted energy facilities in the Kiev region, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19.
Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles at the Kiev region and over 200 drones across the war-torn country, Zelensky said.
“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” Zelensky said on social media.
Last week Kiev said there had been no warning from the United States of similar strikes, leaving virtually no time for residents to take shelter.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied earlier on Oct. 19 that there had been any suspension of intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“There has been no pause,” Rubio told reporters in Uzbekistan when asked about Ukraine’s claims, calling on Zelensky to “focus” on ending the war with Russia.
Trump, who says he has made a deal with Russia to secure fuel exports in exchange for the easing of sanctions, has made renewed attacks on Zelensky in recent days over the war.

But Zelensky in a post on Oct. 19 hit back at the claims, saying that “Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end.”
