articles.title: Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with top US envoys Sunday to try to ease tensions, as Donald Trump accused his counterpart of not wanting to end the war with Russia.
Zelensky spoke to US officials Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other's energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Saint Petersburg since the start of the war in 2022.
Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
On Sunday Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia and Ukraine and making "great progress," but claimed: "Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.
Earlier, after speaking to Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said "a lot depends" on the US position in the war but that "it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end."
Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly", he said. "We expect exactly this approach from all our partners -- both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side."
He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
Zelensky earlier told US broadcaster NBC it would be a "historic mistake" if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would "change his decisions."
But he also said he was "thankful" the US resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.
Thousands without power
A US-led push to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II has so far not brought about a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelensky and Russia's Vladimir Putin because of their lack of progress.
Zelensky spoke to the American officials as he accused Russia of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed.
Ukraine's army launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon -- Russia's second largest retailer -- also reported a strike on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the war.
'Dreadful routine of war'
The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine and, in a fifth year of war, few see a way out of the conflict.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking -- it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
Sergei, another Saint Petersburg resident who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he said.
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.

articles.title: Zelensky seeks further US talks as strikes continue
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Oct. 18 about efforts to end the war and Ukraine’s air defense needs, as Kiev and Washington remained divided over strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Zelensky said they reviewed recent talks between Ukrainian and American teams in Miami and were preparing their next diplomatic steps.
“A great deal depends on America’s position here. Ukraine remains ready to work constructively, honestly, and for real results,” he said.
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and waived new sanctions against Moscow. Zelensky has said Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities continued despite an energy ceasefire announced by the U.S. president.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended Washington’s approach in an Oct. 18 interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” accusing European allies of helping finance Russia’s war through continued purchases of Russian goods.
Bessent put U.S. imports from Russia at $4 billion and said European purchases were more than 10 times higher. He also said European allies had rejected his request to join Washington in imposing tariffs on China and India over their purchases of Russian energy.
“So why should the U.S. bear the burden?” he asked.
Bessent also questioned why European NATO members were not supplying Ukraine with more Patriot air defense systems.
Zelensky separately told Bloomberg that Washington was delaying deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles already paid for through a NATO-coordinated purchasing program. He said he had proposed suspending attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for additional missiles to protect Ukrainian facilities.
The exchanges coincided with further attacks on both sides. Ukrainian drones struck an oil terminal and a fuel depot in St. Petersburg early on Oct. 18, causing fires, Russian officials said. Russian technology company VK said its data center in the neighboring Leningrad region was also targeted.
Russian officials reported one person killed and nine injured in and around St. Petersburg. Zelensky said Russian overnight strikes on Ukraine killed two people and injured 12, while attacks on energy facilities left tens of thousands of households without power.
Further Russian missile strikes hit Kiev late on Oct. 18 and early on Oct. 19. Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that a woman was killed in the first attack. Debris from the subsequent strike damaged metro infrastructure and a residential building, prompting the temporary closure of two stations.

articles.title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.body:
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title: Poland detains reservist suspected of spying on military sites
articles.body:
Jo Harper
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Polish military police have detained a Polish-Ukrainian dual national suspected of carrying out reconnaissance of military installations while attending an officer training course for reservists, officials said Monday.
Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk confirmed that the man was detained at the Military Medical Academy in the central city of Lodz after attracting the attention of Poland’s Military Counterintelligence Service.
“He clearly revealed himself as someone carrying out reconnaissance of certain installations of the Polish Armed Forces,” Tomczyk told reporters.
He stressed that the circumstances are still being investigated and that suspicions of espionage would have to be established through legal proceedings.
The man was detained Friday on the orders of the Lodz-Polesie District Prosecutor’s Office after an investigation by military counterintelligence.
He had acquired Polish citizenship some time previously and also holds Ukrainian citizenship, Tomczyk said. Polish authorities may contact Ukrainian security services as part of the investigation.
The academy confirmed that a participant in its reserve training program had been detained but declined to disclose further details.
According to daily Rzeczpospolita, officers found several cellphones, sets of documents and stamps, large amounts of foreign currency, and gold in the man’s possession. Authorities have not publicly confirmed those details.
A court was expected Monday to consider whether the suspect should be placed in pretrial detention. Polish media said it was not yet known which foreign intelligence service he was suspected of working for.
The case comes amid a series of espionage and sabotage investigations in Poland as Warsaw says foreign intelligence services have increasingly targeted military and critical infrastructure since the start of the Ukraine war in early 2022.
In May, Poland’s Internal Security Agency detained three Polish nationals accused of working for a foreign intelligence service. Investigators said the group had conducted reconnaissance of NATO troop deployments in Poland and had been preparing for possible sabotage operations on instructions from a Russian citizen linked to Russia’s Federal Security Service, or FSB.
More recently, Polish authorities said a September arson attack on a Starlink ground station in central Poland was carried out on behalf of a foreign intelligence service. Investigators also detained another person who had allegedly photographed and filmed the installation and its security arrangements before the attack.

articles.title: Denmark Buys More NSM Missiles, Also Used by Ukraine
articles.body:
Denmark is purchasing an additional batch of Naval Strike Missile (NSM) anti-ship missiles to strengthen the country’s coastal defense.
The Norwegian company Kongsberg announced the deal.
The contract, worth approximately €34.5 million, covers the delivery of an undisclosed number of missiles.
Denmark first acquired NSM-equipped coastal defense systems in 2025, becoming the fifth NATO country to field them, alongside Poland, the United States, Romania, and Latvia. Meanwhile, the Danish Ministry of Defense also ordered these missiles to arm its frigates.
The ordered coastal defense system includes a Kongsberg-developed fire control system, NSM missiles, and launchers.
The Norwegian company Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace began developing the Naval Strike Missile in the 1990s to replace the aging Penguin anti-ship missile. In 2012, the Royal Norwegian Navy officially took the NSM into service.
Over time, NSM missiles have been integrated into the arsenals of the US Navy and Marine Corps, the Polish, Romanian, Latvian and Ukrainian navies, as well as the Royal Navies of the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia.
The NSM is a precision-guided, subsonic, low-observable anti-ship cruise missile by design. It is designed to engage surface vessels with advanced air defense capabilities, as well as land-based targets.
The missile weighs 410 kg and measures 3.9 meters, with about 120 kg in its penetrating blast-fragmentation warhead. The missile’s airframe incorporates radar-absorbing materials to minimize its radar cross-section.
The missile’s propulsion system consists of a solid-fuel booster and a Microturbo TRI 40 turbojet sustainer engine. Its operational engagement range exceeds 500 km.
The NSM’s key feature is its multi-mode guidance system. During the midcourse phase, it uses an inertial navigation system, GPS satellite navigation, and terrain-referenced navigation. In the terminal phase, a passive infrared imaging seeker provides guidance.
Because of its passive infrared seeker, the missile does not emit radio-frequency signals, making it highly resistant to electronic-warfare countermeasures. Its target-recognition algorithms enable the missile to autonomously identify specific vessels, fly at extremely low altitudes, and perform evasive maneuvers during the terminal phase of its flight.

Two presidents, two versions of peace: Trump says Zelensky doesn’t want the war to end. Zelensky says Trump wants Ukraine to give in.

“[W]ith all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump said on his social media platform, Truth Social.
The U.S. president said Zelensky could have “made a better deal two years ago than he can now.” “His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost,” Trump said. He also said Ukraine had lost access to seas and oceans and that its male population had shrunk — “wounded, and/or dead.”
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Zelensky “presents a false binary” by linking an end to the war with a Ukrainian victory. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement, and President Trump is working on that every day. He’s done it since he came into office,” Bessent said in an interview with NBC News.
He also urged Zelensky to “be very careful” about accusing the United States of restricting Starlink in Ukraine. Bessent said those claims were untrue.
Zelensky said Ukraine, rather than Russia, was being pressured to make concessions. “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelensky said in an interview with Bloomberg.
I’m not saying that’s what our partners are trying to achieve. I don’t want to think our American partners believe the war can end sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.

“My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something,” Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president tied the U.S. actions to the November midterm elections, in which Trump is trying to shore up his Republican Party. “Politics is very aggressive during election time,” he said. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue, and I believe it will be calmer.”

articles.title: US Treasury chief rebukes Zelensky for saying Ukraine must win
articles.body:
US Treasury chief rebukes Zelensky
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has rebuked Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky over his insistence that his country must defeat Russia, rejecting his all-or-nothing stance as a “false binary” and insisting that the conflict must end through a negotiated settlement.
Speaking to NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday, Zelensky said Ukraine must win the conflict with Russia, calling victory essential to preserving the country’s independence, geopolitical alignment, and national identity. He lamented that Ukraine “will not prevail” if the US sides with Russia.
“Zelensky presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Bessent told the show shortly after Zelensky’s appearance, arguing that the priority should be ending the conflict rather than determining a winner. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement.”
Bessent stressed that Trump made it clear “he wants to end this war,” noting that the president’s decisions are aimed at securing a negotiated settlement.
Zelensky’s remarks came amid a growing spat with Trump over sanctions on Russian and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. Last week, Trump invoked a national-interest exemption to suspend the sanctions he signed into law last month, including 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
The move followed Trump’s decision days earlier to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports to ease rising fuel prices. According to US media reports, Trump eased the restrictions after Zelensky refused to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which the president blamed for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump – a critical issue just weeks before the US midterm elections. The moves sparked outrage in Kiev, where they were seen as a betrayal of Ukraine’s efforts to maintain Western pressure on Russia.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump defended the moves, saying Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are driving up prices, while stressing that he is focused on brokering a peace deal and does not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” Trump also argued that Zelensky does not want to end the conflict and probably never did, despite receiving billions in Western aid.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov echoed his criticism, suggesting on Sunday that Zelensky has “no desire” to reach a settlement because his government would collapse if Ukraine signed a deal that’s acceptable to both the US and Russia.
Zelensky, whose presidential term expired in 2024, has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Moscow maintains that Zelensky is illegitimate; Trump recently called for his resignation, saying Ukraine should get “a new president.”
Since returning to office, Trump has revived talks with Russia, which were largely suspended under his predecessor, Joe Biden. His efforts to broker peace have produced some results, including POW exchanges, but the diplomatic push has been overshadowed by the US war against Iran and has yet to yield a peace deal.
Moscow has said it would prefer a negotiated settlement. Last month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia expects to hold trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US in the foreseeable future. President Vladimir Putin, however, stressed that the conflict must end on terms that are acceptable to Russia – stressing that a settlement must address the root causes of the conflict and include the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Russian territory, protection for Russian-speakers in Ukraine, as well as denazification and neutral, non-nuclear status for Ukraine.

Trump Eases Russia Sanctions “for Peace” as Zelenskyy Warns of Forced Ukraine Capitulation
US President Donald Trump has defended his decision to suspend sanctions against Russia as an effort to preserve peace negotiations, even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns that Washington’s recent actions increasingly resemble pressure on Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to BBC News on October 19, Trump blocked several sanctions against Russia just two days before they were scheduled to take effect, arguing that imposing additional restrictions could drive Moscow away from negotiations.
“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that he did not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table”.
The decision effectively delayed sanctions previously approved by the US Congress and signed into law in September. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the move as a 60-day suspension intended to assess the potential impact of the restrictions on the American and global economies.
Moscow welcomed the decision. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called it “an important and truly historic moment,” claiming the sanctions would have caused serious damage to the US and global markets.
While the Trump administration presents the suspension as a diplomatic measure, Zelenskyy has raised concerns that Washington’s broader approach could leave Ukraine facing increasing pressure to accept Russian demands.
In an interview with Bloomberg on October 18, Zelenskyy said recent US decisions appeared to be pushing Ukraine toward surrender. “I believe steps were taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president clarified that he was describing the apparent consequences of Washington’s actions rather than accusing American officials of deliberately seeking Ukraine’s surrender.
“I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war can be ended faster at Ukraine’s expense. But that is what it looks like,” he added.
His concerns extend beyond sanctions policy. Zelenskyy cited restrictions on Starlink satellite connectivity, delays in deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles already purchased by Ukraine, and interruptions in intelligence sharing as examples of decisions affecting Kyiv’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
Trump has rejected accusations that Washington deliberately restricted Starlink services or stopped sharing defense intelligence with Ukraine.
The disagreement has also deepened over Washington’s decision to purchase Russian diesel amid rising energy prices linked to the war involving Iran.
Zelenskyy criticized the arrangement, arguing that American purchases of Russian fuel would effectively contribute revenue to Moscow while its forces continue attacking Ukraine.
Despite international sanctions, Russia remains a major oil exporter. According to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, China purchases approximately half of Russia’s crude exports, while India accounts for around 37%.
Trump has also accused Zelenskyy of obstructing negotiations, claiming that the Ukrainian president “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did”.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has maintained that Russia must face sustained international pressure to reach an agreement that does not come at the expense of Ukraine’s sovereignty.
Zelenskyy also said that recent US decisions, including restrictions on military assistance and Starlink connectivity, appeared to be aimed at pressuring Ukraine into capitulation to Russia.
“I believe steps were taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg, while clarifying that he did not necessarily believe Washington intended that outcome.
Zelenskyy also said the US is currently supplying Ukraine with just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, roughly four times fewer than under the Biden administration, while delaying approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for.

articles.title: Massive overnight Russian attack leaves over half a million Ukrainians without power, Zelensky says
articles.body:
More than half a million people across Ukraine are without power due to a massive Russian strike against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure overnight, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X/Twitter on Monday.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelensky wrote. "They again targeted energy facilities and infrastructure, but a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and ordinary residential buildings were also damaged."
"In this one night alone, more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, and the lights went out for at least 550,000 families. Repair crews are working at the sites."
Zelensky added that Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones of various types, including jet-powered Shahed drones.
"Unfortunately, there are casualties," he stated, sending condolences to their families.
Ukraine never wanted war, responded positively to peace attempts
"Ukraine never wanted this war, and we responded positively to literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war honorably—to EVERY ceasefire proposal, our answer was positive," Zelensky continued. "Ballistics, 'Shaheds,' and killings are, again and again, Russia's responses."
"Putin doesn't want not only an end to this war, but even any de-escalatory steps. EVERY one of our partners has faced this personally when hearing refusals from Russia. And it's very important to call things by their proper names. To call the aggressor an aggressor and to help Ukraine protect lives."
Earlier in the day, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Monday its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on targets in Kyiv and Ukraine's capital region, targeting military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and drones, and data centers.

articles.title: Lavrov in Iran as Moscow looks to mediate in war
articles.body:
This file photo shows Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov (R), and Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (L) shaking hands during a meeting in Moscow, Russia.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Iran on Oct. 19 in his first visit since the outbreak of the Middle East war as Moscow seeks to play a mediating role.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said that the trip would focus on “regional and international developments.”
Lavrov was scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and hold talks with his counterpart Abbas Araghchi.
The veteran diplomat has said Moscow’s efforts are “aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war,” with talks stalled between Tehran and Washington.
His visit comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin told Pezeshkian in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Russia and Iran, two of the most heavily sanctioned nations in the world, maintain close ties. Their military and economic cooperation has only increased since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In January 2025, Pezeshkian and Putin signed a 20-year strategic partnership treaty in Moscow, covering cooperation in defense, security, energy, trade and transportation.
The agreement also provides for closer coordination on regional and international issues, although it does not establish a mutual defense obligation.
The Middle East war began in February with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Despite a ceasefire in April, followed by a U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding in June, hostilities in and around the Strait of Hormuz have not stopped.
Iran claims control over the strategic waterway — through which one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons pass in normal times — and regularly targets vessels that cross without its authorisation.
In response, Washington has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said discussions during Lavrov’s visit were expected to focus on “ways to resolve the acute international crisis triggered by the unlawful aggression of the US and Israel against Iran.”
The ministry said the war had been a blow to stability and security “not only in the near and Middle East, but also on a global scale.”
Iran-backed Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz.
The hostilities were the focus of a meeting on Oct. 18 between the Russian and Saudi foreign ministers on the sidelines of a summit between Gulf states and Russia in Bahrain’s Manama.
They discussed “regional developments, particularly the escalation in Yemen, as well as the persistent threats to shipping in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab”, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said on X.
The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport.
A Houthi projectile injured at least six people in southern Saudi Arabia on Oct. 18 after it struck a residential area in Najran near the border with Yemen, according to the kingdom’s civil defence agency.
The Saudi-led coalition also said two ballistic missiles were intercepted in the kingdom’s south. Threat alerts for Najran city and As Sulayyil governorate in Riyadh province were issued but quickly cancelled on Oct. 18.

US Sends Ukraine Just 12 Patriot Missiles a Month, Holds Back Paid-For Supplies, Zelenskyy Says
The United States is supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot air defense interceptor missiles per month—roughly four times fewer than under former President Joe Biden—while withholding approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Bloomberg on October 18, Zelenskyy accused Washington of delaying critical air defense supplies and using restrictions on military assistance to pressure Ukraine into accepting unfavorable terms to end Russia’s war.
“We have paid for the weapons,” Zelenskyy said, referring to purchases that include anti-ballistic missile interceptors under the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. “A part of the supplies has been authorized” by the US side, “while the rest haven’t been. And this is not a technical issue.”
The Ukrainian president said the current delivery rate represents approximately one-quarter of the number of Patriot interceptors supplied during the Biden administration. Unlike previous US military assistance, which provided interceptors to Ukraine without charge, the Trump administration is selling the missiles to Kyiv.
The restrictions come as Ukraine faces continued Russian ballistic missile attacks targeting cities and critical infrastructure, increasing demand for interceptor missiles capable of countering such threats.
Zelenskyy also proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes against Russian diesel fuel production facilities in exchange for additional Patriot interceptors.
“My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg.
The proposal follows US demands that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, which the Trump administration has linked to rising global diesel prices. However, Zelenskyy suggested that Washington’s actions extended beyond disagreements over energy infrastructure.
“I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” he said. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.”
According to Bloomberg, the restrictions on Patriot deliveries have coincided with disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink satellite communications and the absence of advance US warning ahead of a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on October 18.
Despite the current disagreements, Zelenskyy expressed hope that relations with Washington could improve following the November 3 US midterm elections. “Politics is very aggressive during election time,” Zelenskyy told Bloomberg. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue and I believe it will be calmer.”
Earlier, on October 16, Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine was facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles, noting that most available supplies had been redirected to the Middle East.

Russia damaged 28 substations across Ukraine overnight, in addition to other unspecified “important energy facilities,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday afternoon.
Earlier reports estimate that at least 16 Russian ballistic missiles and 269 drones were launched across Ukraine, leading to blackouts for over 550,000 households nationwide.

articles.title: World to face serious energy crisis if US resumes war on Iran
articles.body:
In an exclusive interview with the Tehran Times, IRGC spokesman General Hossein Mohebbi discussed the course of military operations over the past months and what may lie ahead. He also assessed the current state of Iran's armed forces, and spoke personally about succeeding his assassinated predecessor, Martyr General Ali-Mohammad Naeini — and about duty and loss within the faith that sustains Iran's forces on the front lines.
Below is the full text of the interview:
A question that's on a lot of people's minds these days — both in Iran and around the world — is whether the United States and Israel are once again heading toward an escalation of war and conflict, or not. How would you respond to this?
As military forces, we consider every scenario in this regard possible, and from where we stand, no possibility is off the table. That said, based on our assessments, America is definitely not in a position to want to start a new conflict in order to gain some fresh achievement from it. In the past, America came in with everything it had — it had well-equipped bases and vast amounts of equipment at its disposal, it brought fresh, ready-to-fight forces into the field, it pulled out all the stops and drew on every capacity it had — and yet it still couldn't achieve a single one of its declared or undeclared objectives. Not only did it fail, it suffered numerous strategic defeats, the least of which was the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Despite everything America has done so far, it still hasn't been able to reopen that strait, and on top of that, it's suffered enormously significant strategic defeats.
So at this point, America no longer has those capabilities, and it can't use those bases the way it once did. Most of those bases have been shut down, their equipment has been destroyed, and the countries that were most cooperative with America back then no longer offer that same cooperation. American forces today are tired, worn-out forces, and they've pulled back hundreds of kilometers from us. Before the war started, there were at least thirty to forty warships inside the Persian Gulf; but today, not only do they have no ships inside the Persian Gulf, they've also withdrawn roughly seven hundred kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz. The forces that were stationed at those regional bases have now been moved to distant bases, and even at those distant bases — like Al-Azraq and Al-Tanf in Jordan and Syria — they're no longer safe, because those locations too are within our crosshairs.
So from a military capability standpoint and from a technical perspective, America doesn't have what it takes to carry out a new operation or conflict. But there is a possibility that, with the American elections coming up, it might want to manufacture some kind of achievement — for example, carrying out a limited action so it can exploit the results for the elections. That possibility exists, and since we don't dismiss any possibility, we're ready to respond to any action. Our response this time will be far more severe and will land America in far bigger trouble, and will confront the world with even bigger challenges too. In any case, if America takes a new action — even a limited one — the world will face a serious energy crisis. What's happened so far, in our view, hasn't yet reached the stage of a crisis, and we haven't yet brought all our capacity to bear on fully closing the strait. If America wants to make a new move, it will definitely be facing a massive crisis, and it will also confront the world with a new energy crisis.
With the cold season coming up in Europe, and with America itself and many countries needing energy for heating and daily life, the world will face a new crisis, and a global consensus will form against America — a country that creates problems for the whole world by starting fires. Global public opinion is already against America, and if there's any new move, that opposition will only grow, and America will pay a very heavy price. In our view, rationality dictates that they shouldn't do such a thing; but if one day, based on some illusion or delusion of gaining a new achievement, they want to take action, they'll pay a very heavy price. We haven't yet linked up the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab al-Mandab Strait, and the Suez Canal, and we haven't yet used all the capacities of our region — our material and spiritual potential, our popular strength, the capacity of the resistance front, and the other tools that could create a major challenge for America.
So if we look at the story from America's point of view, this scenario seems unlikely, but it's still possible, and it's precisely on the basis of that possibility that we've prepared our scenarios.
That said, when it comes to the Zionist regime, the matter is different. The Zionist regime is, in any case, looking to take advantage of America's companionship and to act even more aggressively. This possibility is worth thinking about from that angle, and this is where the American people need to think. The letter we wrote to the American people has, in part, this very dimension: Are the American people willing, for the sake of following Zionist policies and helping them reach their vile ambitions, to create massive troubles and enormous challenges — like an energy crisis and even a food crisis — for their own country and for the world? I doubt the American people would be willing to accept such a thing, and we pointed to this in that letter as well.
So if I wanted to sum up my words in one sentence, the answer to your question is that the possibility of any operation — even a limited one — is not entirely ruled out, but our assessments show that they simply don't have the capability needed to carry out an effective operation and achieve their goals. Their capability has become so weakened and scattered that they certainly won't get the results they want, and they'll only box themselves into bigger constraints. They might one day take action for the sake of a limited, tactical gain on the eve of the elections, but they'll certainly run into bigger defeats and constraints, global public opinion will mobilize against them, and there are plenty of options available to deter America. The best path and the best proposal for America is to accept Iran's conditions and declare its defeat by accepting those conditions; that would be the best path for the United States.
The enemy is trying to make it seem as though it was Iran that, by attacking several oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, caused the Islamabad MoU to fall apart. They even claimed that a few rogue forces acted without coordination on July 7. Can you tell us what exactly happened that day?
America is doing a forward escape and resorting to sophistry, when in fact the main violator of this agreement was the United States itself. This breach of promise first happened when, right after the meeting where the memorandum of understanding was concluded and sessions were held to implement its provisions, the US Secretary of State took a trip to the region and issued a statement with the leaders of regional countries that was clearly at odds with the provisions of the memorandum. On the other hand, under Article Five of the memorandum, it had been stipulated that the passage of ships would be conducted according to Iranian arrangements, but America, by threatening certain regional countries, opened a new illegal route through the southern part of the strait and along the coast of Oman in order to effectively nullify that article. Not only did they open a new passage, they also forced ships to pass through it and ignored the Iranian arrangements.
This behavior showed that America had once again broken its word — an approach that had precedent. They once carried out the attack of June 13, 2025 during the negotiations, another time they carried out the attack of February 28 in the middle of the negotiation process, and for a third time — not during the talks but after the Islamabad memorandum was concluded and at the stage of implementing it — they violated the agreement. What should the logical response to such a blatant breach of promise be? A logical, powerful, and fitting response. Any fair and reasonable person, if they look at this sequence, will acknowledge that in the face of America's repeated violations, we were compelled to show our decisiveness and strength — something that, praise God, was achieved.
As was seen, during the 17-day clashes, the greatest losses were inflicted on America. In an interview with the Tasnim News Agency, I announced the exact figures for human casualties, destroyed equipment, and demolished bases, because heavy blows were dealt to them as a result of their latest breach of promise. The claim that the actions taken by our forces were rogue is absolutely untrue. In military structures around the world, discipline and adherence to the organizational chain of command is the first principle, and no one can take unilateral action on a sensitive matter like war without coordinating with the higher levels. So our response was carried out with full coordination and as a decisive reaction to America's breach of promise.
The world needs to know that breach of promise is rooted in the very nature of the United States' statecraft, and that this country doesn't adhere to its signatures and commitments. The America that trampled the JCPOA despite the signature of its then-president and five other countries; the America that, during negotiations, assassinated senior commanders, national leaders, and scientists, and massacred thousands of innocent people — has once again proven that violating agreements is part of the fixed procedures of this country's governance. Breach of promise and disrupting agreements have, as it were, become part of the unwritten doctrine of America's ruling establishment.
On this basis, I declare with certainty that our response to the United States' breach of promise — whether in connection to the JCPOA or the recent agreements — was a strong, powerful, fully appropriate, and timely response. If time were to turn back to the 16th of Tir [July 7] we would do exactly the same thing again, and if such actions are repeated by the other side, our response will be even more crushing than before.
Let's talk a bit more about the events of July 7. Some domestic and foreign experts, attempting to corroborate the United States' claim that the attacks that day were rogue, argue that — given Iran's mosaic defense structure, in which commanders of each unit can act without coordinating with higher authorities if necessary — the occurrence of such an incident is not far-fetched. How would you respond to this analysis?
These two matters are completely different from each other. When we talk about a rogue action, we mean an individual acting without orders and without coordinating with higher bodies, and in conflict with standing directives — something that has absolutely no place in the armed forces. But the matter of mosaic defense and delegating authority to commanders in conditions of severed communications or the martyrdom of a senior commander is a defined doctrine and system, not disorder. In this structure, the chain of succession is precisely specified; that is, if the first commander is martyred or organizational communications are cut off through radio, telephone, or communication networks, the next commanders make decisions based on the requirements of the battlefield and a precise assessment of the enemy's situation. This approach is a military measure, and it isn't called rogue action.
Such measures are even rooted in our epistemic and religious foundations; just as in historical military traditions, specific successors were appointed for conditions in which commanders' communications were severed. So a distinction has to be made between the word "rogue action" and "wartime measure." The enemy raising such claims is part of psychological operations aimed at creating a rift between the body of the armed forces and the country's senior officials, or at suggesting a disagreement between the government and military institutions. They've repeatedly raised these rumors to suggest that the decision-making structure in Iran is unclear, but such atmospherics are merely media tricks whose nature is completely clear to experts, and others too have come to understand this reality well over recent months.
You probably meet with field commanders and also visit military headquarters. What's your assessment of the morale of Iranian forces after more than seven months of war?
Honestly, whatever I say about this might seem unbelievable to you, your colleagues, and your listeners, but the reality is that the morale of our combatants — from commanders to operating forces and equipment crews — is at the highest level; to the point that when we go to visit them, we feel weak and ashamed before their will and character. They're present in difficult conditions, despite certain shortages, in hot and humid weather above fifty degrees and in an insecure environment with minimal welfare facilities, with exemplary morale, and they don't utter a single word of complaint or grievance. We, who have ourselves lived through the era of the Sacred Defense [Iran-Iraq war] and have been in this system for years, feel small before the greatness of their morale, and this situation is truly indescribable. We're ready to arrange the preliminaries for a trip so that you and your respected colleagues can go to those areas in person, talk with them, conduct interviews, and tell their stories to the people. Anyone who's gone to these areas has been astonished by their will, their morale, and their interesting and creative initiatives in the areas of defense and offense. Even foreign journalists who are sometimes sent to visit are deeply amazed by this level of sacrifice, patriotism, love for the people, and idealism.
What's your assessment of Iran's missile, drone, and air defense capabilities compared to the beginning of the war?
Our capability has undoubtedly increased greatly, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Just this morning I was in a meeting where they were reporting that our capability has increased at least one and a half times compared to the past; because we never halted our production — never. The enemy, in its foolish imagination, comes and targets some of our centers and facilities and claims, "I destroyed their air force, their navy, and their missile industries," but that's not the case, and the enemy's imagination is foolish. We never stopped producing missiles, drones, and whatever else we needed in this war and will need in the future; not only did we not stop, we expanded it. Today we've brought many other centers into our organization for producing more weapons, creating greater precision in targeting, increasing destructive power, extending the range of weapons, and producing entirely new armaments. We've brought all our capacity to bear, and praise God, we've succeeded very well.
A very important point that I think many people have experienced is that in special conditions, talents emerge. What we've witnessed and experienced firsthand in this war is that in special conditions we achieve things that might be unbelievable even to ourselves, and are certainly unbelievable to others. This is divine grace, and it's due to the sincerity our forces have — those who have come to the field with all their being and selflessly, and have brought their strong will against the enemy. They fight with will, they fight with sincerity, and naturally divine grace helps too. God Almighty says that whoever strives in Our path, We will surely show him the way. God Almighty has shown and continues to show our combatants ways that are unbelievable — ways a person might not have even imagined before. In bottlenecks, in special conditions, in emergency conditions, and in conditions of connection to the infinite divine source, ways, paths, initiatives, and innovations are found that are wonder-making, and if the war continues or escalates again, these wonder-makers will certainly reveal themselves, God willing.
So, given all this, can we conclude that we possess weapons that we have not yet used?
Yes. Naturally, no country reveals all its weapons in the very first stages of battle. To this day, we have also long used weapons that were produced decades ago, and what has been employed during this period has mainly been older reserves and productions. We never use a weapon that should be reserved for more special conditions in less special conditions; naturally, that is how it will be.
Why do some regional countries, even knowing that American bases on their soil will be targeted if used against Iran, still grant the US this permission?
The first and most important point is that these countries have realized that the bases that were supposed to help their security have not helped at all — they have actually endangered their security. That is, what has the existence of a base, for example in Kuwait or Bahrain or any of them, done for that country so far? Nothing! That base has not even been able to defend itself. For example, what benefit has the so-called American naval headquarters and its Fifth Fleet stationed in Bahrain brought to Bahrain so far? No benefit at all — it has actually been to their detriment. They themselves have realized that these bases cannot provide their security, and beyond that, they have understood that America also cannot provide their security; even America cannot provide security for its own forces, and they have come to this truth.
But your question is: now that they have reached this conclusion, why do they not cut off their relations and abandon them? Naturally, they have contracts with them and have given commitments to America — perhaps as reciprocal commitments — and maybe in the back of their minds they still have some hopes regarding America that stop them from acting quickly; but they will do it, and they will do it gradually. What was the first step in this regard? The Mecca Pact. This pact was concluded among three countries — Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan — without foreign interference; this itself shows that they have become disappointed with pacts with foreign countries like America and have seen that they are of no use to them, and so they have turned to a regional pact.
Such regional pacts, and the possible desire of other countries to join them or even to conclude new pacts, stem from the fact that they have concluded that a foreign country thousands of kilometers away cannot provide their security. So, to answer you specifically: they have concluded that they must gradually separate from America and have these bases removed from their countries; but because of their commitments, their not-so-great hopes regarding America, and the limitations they currently have, they cannot do this quickly — but they will gradually bring it about. If the current generation does not do it — which in my view it certainly will — the next generation will one hundred percent accomplish it.
This is a logical, rational, and experienced process. Based on this understanding, new decisions must certainly be made and we must turn to the regional countries themselves. We too, truly, based on the guidelines of the martyred Imam and the esteemed Leader of the Islamic Revolution, have always wanted to be friends, allies, and to have exchanges with these countries. We have many commonalities in this region — generational, religious, cultural, historical commonalities, historical exchanges, and in some cases a shared destiny.
Now, for example, suppose this region becomes insecure for Iran — will security be created for those countries? Never! There will be absolutely no security in this region without Iran's security, and it will not come about. No security pact will take shape in this region without creating security for Iran; this is a logical matter, and empirical processes have proven it.
So we once again declare to the regional countries — we have fifteen neighbors, apart from those somewhat farther away — that these countries must themselves come together, resolve minor differences, and provide their own security. We too are ready to conclude joint pacts with every single country in which American bases are located, and to provide security regionally and locally, and we certainly have this capability.
Recently, the IRGC published a detailed letter addressed to the American people. What was the purpose behind publishing this letter?
In the first place, our goal was to enlighten and inform the American people. We feel that the American people are unaware of many realities; and the reason for this unawareness is that their leaders and ruling establishment lie to them and do not tell them the truth. Their media too are heavily controlled and subservient to the ruling establishment and cannot express other truths contrary to their views. We have numerous examples of this; even in the case of this very letter's publication, many [Western] media outlets boycotted and opposed it, and this shows that they do not allow the facts to reach the ears of the American people. So we wanted through this letter to clarify part of the realities and explain that the American people themselves are also oppressed by their ruling establishment.
That is, the actions America takes, the aggressions it commits against various countries, the massacres it carries out, the numerous bases it has around the world, and the enormous costs it spends to run these bases and forces and equipment — all of it is paid from the pockets of the American people; but the benefit does not reach the American people — rather, it goes into the pockets of the ruling establishment and the main capitalists of America. In other words, the American people today are in the service of American capitalists and Zionist thinking, and we are certain that a large portion of the American people are unaware of this reality.
By the way, what war or enmity do the American people have with the people of Iraq, that a million human beings should be killed over a lie? What enmity do the American people really have with the people of Iran — or conversely, what enmity could the people of Iran possibly have with the American people — that from thousands of kilometers away, they should martyr our leaders, commanders, and scientists, threaten our country with disintegration, plunder our underground resources, threaten to occupy our islands, and target our missile capability? We truly consider it unlikely that these are the wishes of the American people. What real enmity can our two nations have with each other? These actions are in fact carried out by the leaders and ruling establishment of America, and because of their many lies and their concealment of realities from their own people. Our primary goal was in fact to enlighten, inform, and raise awareness among the American people.
You became the successor to General Ali-Mohammad Naeini, who was assassinated by the US and Israel during the 40-day war. Did this cause any doubt for you, or any opposition from your family, regarding accepting this responsibility?
For me personally, such doubt has never existed and doesn't exist; because we've concluded in our school, religion, Quranic teachings, and religious knowledge that we must carry out whatever duty is created for us. When this matter was proposed to me and I felt it was my duty, I didn't hesitate at all and I said to myself: right now this is my duty and I must carry it out. If, on the path of carrying out this duty, God Almighty grants us martyrdom, that's a great triumph; meaning I've lost nothing — rather, I've attained eternal felicity.
So, based on that well-known teaching in our religious knowledge — "one of the two best outcomes" (one of two good things, both of which are good) — if I can carry out my duty well at this juncture, I've attained one of those good things, and blessed be I; and if I'm martyred on this path, I've attained the second good thing, and again blessed be I. That is, in both cases I've lost nothing and in both cases I've gained something; carrying out one's duty well is one felicity, and martyrdom on its path is another felicity, and whichever befalls me is one of those two good things.
Truly, for my family too there was no doubt whatsoever; because my family is far more revolutionary, stronger, and more spirited than I am myself, and in fact, in many of these arenas, they've been our encouragers from the very beginning until now. So martyrdom for me is felicity, and if it befalls me I'll be very happy; and I advise the survivors too to be happy and to take pride.
