articles.title: Hegseth wrong to say most non-US Nato forces in Afghanistan did not fight, says No 10
articles.body:
Downing Street has criticised Pete Hegseth for downplaying the role of Nato allies in helping the US with combat operations in Afghanistan, saying Donald Trump’s defence secretary had been wrong to do so.
The direct condemnation came as No 10 more carefully distanced itself from Trump’s increasing willingness to engage with Russia, saying the UK’s backing for Ukraine was “unwavering”.
Making a speech on Saturday, Hegseth, who served as a Minnesota Army National Guard instructor in Afghanistan, said that when he would go to the coalition base in Kabul, “there would be 50 flags at the headquarters”.
He went on: “And it was a beautiful thing to see, 50 different countries contributing to the Nato alliance and the Isaf [International Security Assistance Force] mission there. Except there were maybe five that contributed. It was actually closer to one or two that actually … by the end were actually involved in kinetic operations.
“In fact, the patch ‘Isaf’ – we joked that it meant ‘I Saw Americans Fighting’. Which is sort of a joke but it’s demoralising when you feel like it’s not burden-sharing, it’s actually a burden.”
While almost 2,500 US forces died in Afghanistan, two-thirds of the total death toll, personnel from more than 30 nations died on duty there, including 457 from the UK.
Asked about Hegseth’s comments, Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson said: “Frankly, the facts speak for themselves when it comes to the UK’s and Nato’s contribution to Afghanistan.
“Thousands of British and allied families made huge sacrifices to play their significant part in that war and uphold our values, and more than 450 British personnel never returned.
“Their sacrifice and that of other Nato forces was made in the service of collective security and in response to an attack on our ally. We are incredibly proud of our armed forces, and their service and sacrifice will never be forgotten. And it is wrong to diminish their role.”
The remarks echo an even more direct rebuke to Trump by Keir Starmer in January, when the then PM said the president should apologise for “insulting and frankly appalling” remarks claiming that Nato troops had stayed “a little back, a little off the frontlines” in Afghanistan.
On Ukraine, Trump has recently renewed his criticisms of the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, eased sanctions on Russia and limited intelligence-sharing that helps Ukraine counter Russian missile and drone attacks.
Asked about reports that the US president wanted to convene a peace summit involving the US, Russia and China, but not Ukraine, the No 10 spokesperson did not respond directly to that, but made clear the UK’s different approach.
He said: “Our position on Ukraine has been consistent since the conflict broke out, and that is that we want Ukraine to secure a just and lasting peace.”
Pushed on the mooted three-way talks, he said: “Well, obviously that’s a matter for those countries, and obviously for Ukraine to speak for itself.”
The spokesperson added: “Our support for Ukraine is unwavering, and I think you saw that in the prime minister’s meeting with President Zelenskyy last week.”

articles.title: US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches
articles.body:
US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not confirm reports that Ukraine received no advance warning before Russia's ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 19, citing a lack of information, as he spoke to reporters during a visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu asked Rubio during a press briefing to comment on Kyiv's statements that it had received no advance warning of Russian missile launches.
"I don't know. I mean, where did it happen last night? I don't know exactly," Rubio told reporters on Oct. 19.
In the Oct. 19 attack on Kyiv, at least one person was killed, and eight others were injured as Russian missiles struck Kyiv in multiple waves overnight. Explosions were reported shortly before 11 p.m., followed by further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m. local time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X on Oct. 19 that Ukraine had not received early warning from its partner countries, including the U.S., ahead of the attack. He added that Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region as the primary targets.
Later in the day, Ukraine's Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on national television that Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners before the first wave of ballistic missile attacks at around 11 p.m., but that information about the second wave, at around 3 a.m., was provided.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes overnight on Oct. 19, though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that "a few nights ago" there was a software problem involving the Ukrainian early warning system.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back. I can't comment on what happened last night," he said.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first overnight wave followed a similar pattern.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened," the official said. "They're up to something again."
It can be common for Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles to hit with very little advance warning.
The attack came just hours after Zelensky said the U.S. had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine about Russian missile launches.
The president's announcement came as a relief after Kyiv endured "massive explosions" on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack came after the U.S. threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries, sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials have previously explained that satellite surveillance of launch sites can be vulnerable to transmission delays. Bad weather may also cause interference with the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellites, a surveillance network U.S. forces use to monitor Russian launch sites.
But the senior official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said although bad weather had affected warnings before, this number of strikes with little to no warning "has never happened before."
"Now we're seeing 'bad weather' three times in a row," the official said. "When nothing comes through on any channel... well, we get it."

articles.title: Most Ukrainians reject giving Russia all of Donbas. Support for resistance on rose to 62% after new US pressure, poll finds
articles.body:
A majority of Ukrainians reject handing all of Donbas to Russia in exchange for US and European security guarantees. Some 62% are ready to endure the war for as long as it takes, a survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology shows.
Russia has spent the fall hammering Ukrainian cities, and Washington has eased sanctions on Russian diesel and cut Ukraine’s intelligence and Starlink speed, both apparently aimed at wearing Ukrainians down toward a capitulation. Instead, the majority calls the withdrawal of troops from Donbas categorically unacceptable, with 35% willing to accept it and 4% undecided, a position essentially unchanged since late summer.
The pressure campaign tracked the other way. Among those polled on 8-9 October, before the diesel deal and the pressure that followed, 57% were categorically opposed. Among those polled on 10-16 October, the figure rose to 62% afterward, KIIS reports.
In every region, at least half reject the trade. Resistance is firmest in Kyiv, which has borne a relentless campaign of ballistic and jet-drone strikes, where 66% are categorically against, the highest figure of any region. Even in the east, around Kharkiv, where the most are open to a compromise at 45%, 51% still rule it out.
Bracing for a long war, and ready for it
Few Ukrainians expect a quick end. Only 10% think the war will end by the close of 2026 and 13% in the first half of 2027, while 56% expect it to run into the second half of 2027 or beyond, the institute reports.
Who Ukrainians blame for blocking peace
The poll also measured who is seen as the obstacle. Asked to choose, 78% said Russia’s drive to subjugate Ukraine is what blocks peace, against 12% who blamed an inflexible Ukrainian government, and 92% said Russia strikes economic sites to wreck the economy and force capitulation, not in retaliation.
“The enemy, with its vile strikes by ballistic missiles and drones, is unable to break the spirit and will of Ukrainians,” KIIS executive director Anton Hrushetskyi says.
He argues that what Ukraine needs is “packages of interceptors for Patriot systems,” not an election or one-sided concessions dressed up as peace. The survey polled 1,031 adults across government-controlled Ukraine from 8-16 October.

articles.title: Congressman from Trump's party threatens administration with consequences over Starshield restrictions for Ukrainian Armed Forces
articles.body:
Congressman from Trump's party threatens administration with consequences over Starshield restrictions for Ukrainian Armed Forces
US Representative Brian Fitzpatrick (Republican) has warned that those involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the Starshield program will be held fully accountable.
Source: European Pravda, citing Fitzpatrick on X (Twitter)
Details: The congressman announced talks with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his team this week to discuss the Starshield program, sanctions, and other matters pertaining to the defence of Ukraine.
Fitzpatrick noted that during the conversation, he will assure Zelenskyy that US officials involved in restricting the program for Ukraine will face consequences from Congress.
Quote from Fitzpatrick: "I will be assuring President Zelenskyy that anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings, and immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head."
Details: Fitzpatrick mentioned his bill, the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act, which aims to prevent US President Donald Trump from unilaterally lifting sanctions on Russian oil. He expressed confidence that the House of Representatives will approve this initiative.
Quote from Fitzpatrick: "The United States must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself. The United States must not import a single drop of Russian oil. Sanctions against the Russian regime must be harsher and stronger than they've ever been before. Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor – and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin.
This is, after all, what Ronald Reagan would do. And this is what we will do now. Ukraine can, and will, defeat Russia."
Details: Fitzpatrick reiterated that Ukraine is an indispensable ally of the US, while Russia is an enemy of Washington, and assured Kyiv of continued support.
Background:
- Following the US-Russia "diesel deal", Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick introduced a bipartisan bill that he says will prevent Trump from lifting sanctions; it was named the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump claims he did not give an order to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX's Starshield satellite technology.

articles.title: Trump Endorses Netanyahu Days Before Israeli Election as Iran War Tests Friendship
articles.body:
With days to go before a crucial general election in Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received a last-minute endorsement for re-election on Sunday from his longtime friend, U.S. President Donald Trump.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump posted on Truth Social Sunday. “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
It’s a ringing, albeit late, recommendation for someone Trump hasn’t seen eye-to-eye with in recent months over how Netanyahu’s government has navigated the Middle East conflict. Trump explained his delayed endorsement to Axios reporter Barak Ravid, saying that he’d always meant to endorse Netanyahu because they “have a good relationship, and because we’ll continue to do good things together.”
Trump said in his post that, if Israel were to have “the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi,” the U.S. would be left alone to face the Iran threat. The U.S. and Israel jointly struck Iran in late February, kickstarting a conflict that has not only upended global markets but also thrust Middle Eastern regional security into turmoil.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump added, in apparent reference to Netanyahu’s domestic challenges, including a corruption trial, some of which the U.S. President has previously tried to influence. “Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he has thrived!”
Trump’s endorsement comes just before Israelis head to the polling booths on Oct. 27, some three years after the country’s war with terror group Hamas ignited. Since then, Netanyahu has been criticized by opponents for failing to deliver on his promise of restoring regional security.
Public disillusionment with Netanyahu was among several factors that led to the formation of the Yashar! (“Straight!”) Party, whose founder, former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, is challenging Netanyahu for the premiership. Eisenkot’s son and nephews were killed in the war in the Gaza Strip.
It’s unclear how big of an electoral boost Netanyahu will get from Trump’s endorsement. An opinion poll from nonprofit The Jewish People Policy Institute in Jerusalem released this month shows that most Israelis still see Trump as a great friend of Israel. A separate opinion poll from JPPI, however, shows their trust in him has eroded. Eisenkot, reacting to Trump’s endorsement, said at an event in Tel Aviv that while he appreciates Trump, only Israelis will decide on their next Prime Minister. Some surveys show Yashar! is in a tight race with Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party.
Netanyahu nonetheless thanked his “dear friend Donald” in a video posted on social media, saying he was “honored” and “humbled” by Trump’s backing, adding that the U.S. was “fortunate” to have Trump as its leader in the fight to denuclearize Iran.
Trump and Netanyahu’s fraught friendship
Even before Trump became U.S. President, he had publicly endorsed Netanyahu, though Trump, still only a TV personality in 2013, said that the Israeli politician asked for it. Since Trump was first elected, the two have been political allies and friends. Their relationship, however, has seen a number of ups and downs since Trump returned to the White House last year.
Netanyahu was the first foreign leader invited to the White House during Trump’s second-term Administration, and he has met with Trump repeatedly since. Netanyahu pushed Trump to target three key Iranian nuclear facilities in June last year. Last November, Trump sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, asking him to pardon Netanyahu on his drawn out corruption trial, which the U.S. President deemed to be “political, unjustified prosecution.”
On Feb. 11, when Trump and Netanyahu met in a closed-door meeting at the White House, Israel and the U.S. failed to reach an agreement on how to proceed with Iran. Netanyahu has long sought to decapitate the Iranian leadership, but Trump at the time insisted on negotiations. Netanyahu, nonetheless, reportedly pressed Trump to launch the Iran operation later that month.
Since their last meeting, their relationship has markedly shifted. Trump has since tried to find an off-ramp to the war in Iran, but Israel’s actions made such peace deal talks thorny.
In March, after Israel attacked Iran’s South Pars gas field in the Persian Gulf, Trump said he told Netanyahu to stop such attacks. Then, on April 17, Trump declared on Truth Social that Israel was “PROHIBITED” from further bombing Lebanon, where it was at war with the militant group Hezbollah. Netanyahu, however, insisted that Israeli troops would remain in southern Lebanon and that security threats persisted—complicating Washington’s efforts toward peace as Tehran indicated that any deal would need to include a halt of the attacks in Lebanon.
When Netanyahu in June ordered strikes on a Hezbollah stronghold in Beirut to retaliate against the group’s alleged attacks on Israel, Trump phoned and excoriated the Israeli Prime Minister, reportedly calling him “f-cking crazy.” Asked by CNBC about the call, Netanyahu said: “We have common goals. Sometimes we have, as in the best of families, you have these tactical disagreements. We always find a way to work them out, and we do so as great friends.”
During Netanyahu’s seventh U.S. visit in July, Trump went public with his frustration. During a telephone interview on Fox News, Trump criticized Netanyahu over reports that the Israeli leader planned to share intelligence showing Iran rebuilding its nuclear program. The U.S. President said: “I don’t need Bibi to tell me that. Bibi is telling me that because he wants me to stay involved.”
Netanyahu is part of Trump’s U.N. alternative called the Board of Peace, though Israel broke again with the U.S. President by rejecting having Turkish and Qatari representatives on the board’s subpanel, the Gaza Executive Board, which is tasked with overseeing post-war reconstruction in the Gaza Strip.
Then Netanyahu rejected the Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to advance a cease-fire in the Gaza Strip and insisted that Israel would not withdraw before Hamas fully disarmed.
In Trump’s extensive interview with TIME in late September, Trump did not answer directly when asked repeatedly if the Israeli population should give Netanyahu another term. “I can only say that I’m not involved in politics anymore,” the U.S. President said.
But despite the lack of clear endorsement then, Trump seemed confident that “Bibi” could still win. “People have written off Bibi many, many times, just like they’ve written off me many, many times,” Trump told TIME. “I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.”

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending war: Rubio
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia should focus on ending their war, as Washington continues efforts to broker a peace deal.
Asked during a visit to Uzbekistan about a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss the four-year-old conflict, Rubio said the meeting had not been confirmed.
“There’s been talks of a meeting. I don’t know whether it’s been finalized, but the president has been clear. He’d like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end,” Rubio told reporters.
Rubio also denied that Washington had suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contrary to claims from Kiev. He called President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to "focus" on ending the war with Russia.
"What he should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war," he said.
Rubio arrived in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet senior officials from the C5+1 grouping, which brings together the US and five Central Asian countries: Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
Trump hosted the leaders of the five countries at the White House last November.
“We see nothing good coming from this war,” Rubio said, warning of the risk of escalation and the conflict spreading into neighbouring countries.
He cited the possibility of a failed sabotage attack or drones affected by electronic warfare straying across borders.
Peace efforts amid renewed attacks
The US has been seeking to mediate an agreement to end the war. Trump has also secured a deal allowing Russian diesel imports and waived some sanctions on Moscow, saying the moves could help keep the Kremlin at the negotiating table.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised the moves.
Meanwhile, a fresh Russian air strike killed a woman in Kiev overnight and hit a subway station, while also damaging a 25-storey residential building, according to the supplied report.

articles.title: From Tehran, Lavrov urges return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Lavrov urges return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz during Iran visit
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has called for conditions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region to return to what they were before the US-Israeli war on Iran, following talks with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Monday.
Speaking at a joint press conference, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow's strategic partnership with Tehran and said Russia remained committed to its comprehensive cooperation agreement with Iran.
He described the talks as "productive" and said the two countries shared similar positions on regional developments, while pledging to continue cooperation through international organisations including BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Eurasian Economic Union.
Lavrov also announced that Russian personnel would gradually return to Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant.
The developments come as diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation intensify, with The New Arab reporting on Monday that a breakthrough in US-Iran mediation efforts could be announced this week.
Senior sources familiar with negotiations told TNA that Qatar and Pakistan were working to narrow differences between Washington and Tehran and secure mutual concessions, while ruling out an immediate military escalation.
Lavrov's visit, his first to Iran since the US-Israeli war began on 28 February, follows Moscow's recent involvement in exchanging messages between the two countries.
It also comes ahead of a possible visit to Tehran by Pakistan's army chief, General Asim Munir, who has been involved in mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran.
Iran and Russia blame US-Israeli attacks for regional instability
Araghchi described Iran's relationship with Russia as "strategic", saying it had taken on new dimensions since the implementation of their comprehensive cooperation agreement nearly two years ago.
He said Monday's discussions had been "extremely productive", covering regional and international developments alongside practical plans to expand political, cultural and commercial cooperation.
The Iranian foreign minister said economic ties between the two countries were developing significantly and that no major obstacles stood in the way of expanding bilateral trade.
On regional security, Araghchi blamed US and Israeli military attacks for instability in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, as well as recent security incidents in the Caspian Sea involving attacks on Iranian and Russian vessels and port infrastructure.
He warned that the situation posed serious consequences for regional peace, security and the environment.
Araghchi also called for an immediate end to the genocide in Palestine, Israeli expansion in Lebanon and the war in Yemen.
The two ministers discussed tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan, including the need to reduce tensions between Kabul and Islamabad and address threats from armed groups operating in Afghanistan.
Araghchi stressed that regional disputes could not be resolved through military means and required diplomacy and political solutions.
Lavrov, meanwhile, said opposition to US unilateralism remained a shared priority for Moscow and Tehran, with both countries seeking to strengthen multilateral institutions and uphold international law.
He also reaffirmed Russia's commitment to its comprehensive cooperation agreement with Iran.
Can Russia mediate between Iran and the US?
Despite the emphasis on regional diplomacy, neither minister publicly announced a new Russian mediation initiative between Washington and Tehran following Monday's talks.
Russia's potential mediation role began taking shape earlier this month, amid growing contacts between Moscow and Washington over the war in Ukraine.
On 10 October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov revealed that Russian President Vladimir Putin had informed his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian of an upcoming telephone conversation with US President Donald Trump.
The exchange followed a meeting between Putin and Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on 9 October.
The Kremlin subsequently announced that Putin had conveyed Iran's position on a possible settlement to Trump, raising expectations that Moscow could become another diplomatic channel between Washington and Tehran.
However, Iranian officials have stopped short of recognising Russia as a formal mediator.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said last week that, "technically, in the strict sense of the word", Pakistan and Qatar remained the actual mediators between Iran and the United States.
He added that consultations between Tehran and Moscow, particularly on the nuclear issue, were nothing new.
Ahead of his arrival in Tehran, Lavrov criticised Trump's approach towards Iran as "wrong", arguing that it would not help achieve an agreement based on mutual respect and international law.
His visit followed a stop in Bahrain, prompting speculation that he could also be carrying messages from Gulf states amid heightened regional tensions.
Experts question prospects of Russian mediation
Iranian analyst Hadi Mohammadi told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected growing Russian concerns about developments in the Gulf and the possibility of further escalation.
He said Moscow appeared to be intensifying its diplomatic activities in an attempt to contain tensions, noting that the US-Iran confrontation had become closely linked to the war in Ukraine amid renewed contacts between Washington and Moscow.
Mohammadi suggested that Lavrov could be carrying messages from Washington or Israel during what he described as an extremely sensitive period.
He recalled that Putin had previously conveyed messages between Tehran and Israel, including an Israeli assurance before the latest war that it did not intend to attack Iran.
However, Mohammadi expressed limited confidence in Russia's ability to secure a breakthrough.
He argued that some international actors were making a fundamental mistake by pressuring Iran alone to accept the other side's conditions, while overlooking Tehran's position that it had been attacked and had complied with the Islamabad memorandum of understanding reached in June, which Iran accuses Washington of violating.
Mohammadi said Lavrov's visit could help reduce regional tensions but was unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.
At best, he suggested, it could mark the beginning of further diplomatic exchanges, although he did not rule out the possibility that it represented a final attempt to avert another war.
Iranian analyst Abbas Aslani similarly told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected the depth of cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in confronting Western pressure.
He said shared economic, political and military challenges had strengthened the importance of bilateral and regional coordination.
Aslani considered it possible that Lavrov was carrying a response or message from Washington, although he cautioned against drawing conclusions before the talks took place.
He also suggested that Moscow could use the visit to assess the Trump administration's position ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November.
According to Aslani, Russia was already familiar with Iran's strategic red lines, including the conditions outlined in Tehran's seven-day proposal, and was unlikely to persuade Iranian officials to make substantial changes.
He described the visit as a potential opportunity to exchange "hard truths", but argued that any genuine breakthrough would depend on Washington accepting what he described as the new balance of power and security in the Gulf.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defenses fail to intercept single Russian ballistic missile overnight
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. The air defense systems deployed by Ukraine overnight night failed to intercept a single Russian ballistic missile, according to data published by the Ukrainian Air Force on its Telegram channel.
On Monday morning, the Russian Defense Ministry reported that strikes had been carried out overnight against targets in Ukraine, including military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, and a data center in Kiev and the Kiev Region.
Earlier, The Washington Post reported that the Ukrainian military had nearly depleted its stockpile of Patriot missiles, and that deliveries have been irregular since May. For its part, CNN reported that Kiev had been warning its partners for several months that it was running out of Patriot interceptor missiles, which are currently in short supply everywhere.

articles.title: 'We will fight' — We asked Ukrainian soldiers about Trump's latest outburst
articles.body:
'We will fight' — We asked Ukrainian soldiers about Trump's latest outburst
A soldier from a separate task force rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko / Ukrinform / Future Publishing via Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 18 claimed his approach to ending the war in Ukraine is "very simple."
In a post on Truth Social, Trump explained that his decision to ease sanctions on Russia while simultaneously piling pressure on Ukraine was to avoid "foolishly (driving) Russia away from the bargaining table."
For many of Trump’s critics in Ukraine, his recent decisions are viewed in similarly simple terms — Trump is helping Russia win the war.
Trump also doubled down on his criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, and appeared to suggest that Ukraine's position in the war was untenable.
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!"
But as Russia escalates its aerial bombardment of Ukraine's cities, its forces remain largely stuck on the front lines.
And as Operation Vivaldi has shown, in some sectors Moscow's troops are actually going backwards.
The Kyiv Independent asked X Ukrainian soldiers what they thought about Trump's latest outburst…
Some soldiers asked to be identified by callsign or first name only for security reasons.
Bohdan, 
a serviceman
The enemy has not achieved any successes that would suggest a victory on their part. Civilians are the most susceptible to a decline in morale — especially lately, as Russia has been launching mass strikes against civilian infrastructure.
I wouldn't take Trump's words seriously.
He is a media-focused, overly talkative, choleric, elderly, and unwell man.
Artem Kariakin, 
soldier and former partisan
In my opinion, Trump is seeking to bring the fighting in Ukraine to an end by any means necessary, including through Ukraine’s capitulation. He confidently declared to the entire world that he would stop the war in Ukraine, yet year after year he has failed to do so. People no longer believe these claims, and consequently, his slogan that "this war would never have happened under my presidency" is also raising more and more doubts.
It is absolutely clear to me that he is concerned primarily with his own image and approval ratings. That is why he has repeatedly threatened Ukraine — a country that is defending itself against aggression and fighting for its own land. I do not think Trump is genuinely interested in the actual situation on the battlefield. He can easily take Putin’s claims at face value when Putin says that Russia controls certain Ukrainian towns and cities that Russian forces have been unable to reach for years.
I never thought I would see the day when the Russian population, living under the constant influence of propaganda, would be more skeptical of Putin’s claims than the American president.
As for morale at the front, we are not giving up. By now, we have grown accustomed to Trump’s statements and his constantly shifting attitude — from threats against Putin one day to threats against Zelenskyy the next. But when it came to the situation with Starlink, for example, most of us were stunned.
Any restrictions affecting the main communication tool we rely on at the front are not a way of forcing us into a ceasefire at any cost. They are a shove in the back of every one of us, putting our lives at risk. When our hands are tied and we are prevented from defending our own lives and the lives of our loved ones, it hits us hard psychologically. It is not merely a slap in our faces; it is a slap in the face of the entire civilized world.
read also
I hope Trump abandons the idea of using our lives as leverage and understands that we will continue fighting to the end regardless. Otherwise, he risks going down in history as the president who betrayed the entire civilized world.
Returning to the situation on the battlefield, Russia has clearly become bogged down along the front line and is retreating in some sectors. And, as if by some cruel law of nature, every time Russia begins to lose the initiative on the battlefield, those whom we thought were our allies start putting obstacles in our way.
It is especially painful to watch this happen at a time when Putin, faced with the hopelessness of Russia’s situation on the battlefield, has shifted almost entirely toward a strategy of terror against Ukrainian civilians. He is no longer betting on victory at the front — having realized that he cannot defeat the Ukrainian army — but instead on breaking and defeating our civilian population.
But President Trump, and the international community as a whole, must understand one thing — in February 2022, I picked up a weapon and went out to defend Kyiv without even having a helmet or proper body armor. All I had was a Kalashnikov light machine gun, while massive columns of the Russian army were advancing toward our district of the capital. There were many of us like that.
Back then, there was no talk of Starlink or Tomahawks. We went into battle fully aware of how slim our chances were, prepared to fight off an enormous enemy army with little more than our bare hands.
Today, we have a massive army of our own, our own weapons and strike capabilities, and technologies that many countries around the world cannot replicate.
Even if the entire world turns its back on us, we will still stand and fight for our country — because we are Ukrainians.
Illia,
a serviceman in an air assault brigade
In my opinion, the best option is to achieve peace along the current line of contact. The main priority is to stop the bloodshed and save lives.
Morale is dropping every day.
Those who have been fighting since the very beginning are exhausted, and few have any desire to continue. Especially when faced with such injustice.
Trump acts in his own country's interests; for them, it is better if this war ends, as it yields nothing positive. In this situation, neither side — neither us nor Russia — will win, so it is difficult to discuss any clear outcome.
As for why he is pressuring us rather than Russia — I suspect it is simply because we are the weaker party.

articles.title: Trump suggests someone other than Zelenskyy should negotiate for Ukraine
articles.body:
Rabia Iclal Turan
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
US President Donald Trump said Monday that it may be time for someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to negotiate on Kyiv's behalf.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about. Zelensky is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago," Trump told reporters before departing the White House.
"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine because what's happened? A tremendous number of people are dead. They're losing their male population," he said.
"Maybe it's time for Zelensky to get somebody else to negotiate," Trump added.
"Zelensky is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing," he added.
 
Possible talks with Putin, Xi
Asked whether he had agreed to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Ukraine, Trump said he had not but was open to such talks.
"No, but I would do it. Not so much for Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said.
Trump indicated that nuclear disarmament would be a priority in any such meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," he said.
"We have more nuclear weapons than anybody. Russia is second, China is third, but catching up. China was way behind, and now they're catching up. It'll take about probably five years," Trump added.
Asked whether he would meet Putin and Xi to discuss ending the war without Zelenskyy present, Trump said he would do "anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not."
 
Russia, China and Iran
Trump also said Russia and China had provided limited support to Iran despite their close relations with Tehran.
"Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia's done very little for Iran. China could have done a lot more for Iran," he said.
"I view that as being a very positive thing," Trump added.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
But the Ukrainian President also stressed that he does not believe Ukraine’s US partners necessarily intend that outcome.

articles.title: Israel prepared to attack Iran without US – Netanyahu
articles.body:
Israel prepared to attack Iran without US – Netanyahu
Israel is prepared to attack Iran without US participation if necessary, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said, pledging to overthrow Tehran’s government and make striking first a central principle of his security doctrine.
The declaration comes amid ongoing indirect negotiations over the war launched by the US and Israel in February. Israel, a major recipient of American military funding and weapons, has justified its offensives on security grounds, even as the conflict has spread across the region, disrupted Hormuz shipping, and driven up global energy prices.
Presenting his security doctrine in a speech on Sunday, Netanyahu argued that Iran would rebuild its nuclear and military capabilities as long as its government survived and made clear that Israel was prepared to launch further attacks without waiting for American participation.
“If we need to act alone, we will act alone,” he said.
Netanyahu presented Israel’s earlier campaign against Iran as a model, recalling that he told US President Donald Trump he would attack Tehran “either way” and invited American participation in a strike on the Fordow nuclear facility.
He framed further action against Iran as unfinished business, explicitly identifying the overthrow of the country’s government as the ultimate objective. “We are working on it and we will do it,” Netanyahu said.
Despite Tehran repeatedly stressing that its nuclear program is peaceful and denying seeking nuclear weapons, Netanyahu once again claimed that the US-Israeli attacks had prevented Iran from acquiring an atomic bomb intended to destroy Israel.
Netanyahu framed the renewed strikes as part of a broader doctrine prioritizing attack over defense. He compared striking first to gaining the advantage in childhood street fights and said Israel could establish bases far beyond its borders.
“We will have to live by our sword in order to live for many years,” he said.
He also described plans to seize and destroy what he called threat centers in the occupied West Bank, listed preventing Palestinian statehood as a fundamental principle, and included disrupting military and “civilian systems” in his deterrence strategy.
US-Iran negotiations are already deadlocked. Trump rejected Tehran’s proposal last month as “unacceptable,” insisting the US blockade had left Iran “losing so badly” and seeking a deal on Washington’s terms.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated on Saturday that normal shipping in the Strait of Hormuz could resume within seven days if Washington accepted Tehran’s conditions, including lifting the naval blockade, easing oil export restrictions, releasing frozen assets, and ending hostilities on all fronts, including Israel’s operations in Gaza and Lebanon.
Trump has nevertheless threatened renewed bombing, with Axios recently reporting that US officials expected major combat operations could resume after November’s midterm elections.
Tehran has warned that another attack would trigger broader retaliation, potentially targeting American technology infrastructure across the Gulf.

articles.title: Exclusive: Breakthrough expected in US-Iran mediation efforts
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Breakthrough expected in US-Iran mediation efforts this week
A breakthrough in mediation efforts between the United States and Iran is expected to be announced this week, sources familiar with the negotiations told The New Arab on Monday, as Qatar and Pakistan continue diplomatic efforts to prevent a renewed war between Washington and Tehran.
Senior sources familiar with the mediation efforts, speaking to The New Arab on condition of anonymity, said negotiations were continuing to narrow differences and encourage mutual concessions aimed at preventing another military confrontation.
Despite ongoing threats exchanged between Washington and Tehran, and concerns that the war with Iran could resume after the US midterm elections on 3 November, the sources ruled out an immediate escalation in the region.
The anticipated breakthrough comes amid mounting tensions over Iran's nuclear programme, the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz and US demands for Tehran to curb its uranium enrichment capabilities.
On Saturday evening, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth warned that Iran would face "destruction" unless it abandoned its nuclear ambitions at the negotiating table.
Speaking at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville, Hegseth accused Iran of building a "large arsenal" of conventional missiles and attempting to pursue a strategy similar to that of North Korea.
Meanwhile, US embassies across the region have warned of the possibility of rapidly developing security threats, including potential attacks by Iran and its regional allies.
Iran accuses Netanyahu of pushing for another war
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of attempting to drag the United States into another war with Tehran to avoid imprisonment.
Responding to remarks made by Netanyahu about Iran, Araghchi wrote on X that the Israeli leader was "dragging the United States into a new war to avoid going to prison", while disregarding the potential consequences for Israel and the US president.
The Iranian foreign minister also reiterated Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, provided Washington meets several Iranian demands.
These include lifting the blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and halting hostilities across regional fronts.
Araghchi said Tehran had received US feedback on the proposal and was reviewing it, although significant disagreements continued to obstruct progress.
According to Reuters, one of the main sticking points remains Washington's insistence on placing Iran's nuclear programme at the centre of negotiations, including demands for substantial reductions in Tehran's uranium enrichment capabilities.
Iran, however, wants to prioritise reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing the economic and security restrictions imposed on the country.
Qatar and Pakistan intensify mediation efforts
Qatar and Pakistan have continued diplomatic efforts to bridge differences between Washington and Tehran, although political and security obstacles have so far prevented an agreement that could end the confrontation and restore regional stability.
The talks come amid growing concerns over the consequences of the Strait of Hormuz remaining closed, with disruptions to shipping and global energy supplies adding urgency to efforts to reach a settlement.
Iran's ISNA news agency reported on Sunday that Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, could visit Tehran this week as part of ongoing cooperation between the two countries and discussions concerning regional developments and US-Iran negotiations.
The Strait of Hormuz remains one of the central issues in the crisis because of its strategic importance to global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments.
Reopening the waterway could serve not only as a measure to restore maritime traffic but also as an initial confidence-building step towards reducing tensions and restarting negotiations on broader disputes.
However, Tehran's proposal remains conditional on Washington meeting its demands, while the United States continues to insist that concerns over Iran's nuclear programme must be addressed.
Disagreements over sanctions, the blockade on Iranian ports and mechanisms for ending hostilities across the region also remain unresolved.
The latest mediation efforts therefore present Qatar and Pakistan with a critical challenge of preventing the collapse of diplomatic contacts while securing reciprocal confidence-building measures that could pave the way for broader negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and regional security arrangements.
The sources' assessment that an immediate escalation is unlikely offers a potential opening for diplomacy, despite the continued exchange of threats and the absence of a comprehensive agreement between Washington and Tehran.

articles.title: Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)

Russia and India wrap up joint naval drills in Pacific (VIDEO)
Russian and Indian warships have completed joint naval drills off Russia’s Pacific coast, conducting live-fire exercises and practicing defenses against drone attacks as part of the wider Indra-2026 military exercise.
The maritime phase of the drills took place in the Gulf of Peter the Great near Vladivostok, involving the Russian Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Saturday.
INS Sahyadri arrived in Vladivostok on October 10 and conducted harbor engagements before operations at sea.
The crews fired naval artillery at surface and aerial targets, carried out coordinated maneuvers, and tested communications between the vessels. They also practiced repelling attacks by unmanned boats and aerial drones representing a simulated enemy. The Russian corvette used 30mm automatic guns, small arms, and electronic warfare systems to counter the simulated threats.
The exercises culminated in a simulated joint operation to rescue a civilian vessel seized by pirates. Russian and Indian naval counterterrorism units boarded the vessel and neutralized the attackers, with drone operators coordinating their movements.
The two navies also practiced helicopter operations, including reconnaissance, cross-deck landings, and medical evacuations.
An Indian helicopter landed aboard the Russian corvette shortly after a Russian helicopter took off. The crews then exchanged mannequins representing wounded sailors as part of a casualty evacuation exercise, RT correspondent Igor Zhdanov reported from aboard the Russian warship.
Indra-2026 began on October 14 and involves land, naval, and air forces from both countries.
The land component will continue in Russia’s Chelyabinsk Region until October 23, with troops practicing joint command and control and operations against simulated armed groups. Russian and Indian aircrews are also conducting exercises involving Su-30SM fighter jets and Mi-8 helicopters.
The previous edition of the exercise was held off the coast of the southern Indian city of Chennai.
The deployment builds on the longstanding defense partnership between Moscow and New Delhi and carries forward cooperation discussed during Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India last December, India’s Defense Ministry said.

articles.title: Sudan drone strike kills 11 at displacement camp – official
articles.body:
Sudan drone strike kills 11 at displacement camp – official
Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed at least 11 people, including nine children, in a drone attack on a displacement camp in West Darfur, according to the region’s Health and Social Welfare Minister, Babiker Hamdin.
In a statement published on Sunday, Hamdin said that the attack targeted displaced civilians on the Sudan-Chad border. According to preliminary figures, the victims included nine children aged between five and ten and two women aged 23 and 36. Five others were injured.
The victims had reportedly fled their villages last year after RSF fighters allegedly burned and looted their homes. They subsequently sought refuge in Sanakit, near the Chadian border, where they were living in difficult humanitarian conditions before the latest attack.
Hamdin condemned the strike as “a horrific crime and a grave violation of international humanitarian law, reflecting the militia’s indifference to the lives of innocent people.”
He called on the international community to hold those responsible accountable and designate the paramilitary group as a terrorist organization.
Sudan was plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
The RSF has faced similar accusations from rights groups over attacks on civilians. In September, the Sudanese Alliance for Rights reported that five people were killed in an attack on a market in North Kordofan, while the Committee for Justice blamed the group for a courthouse strike that killed ten. On October 9, the Sudan Doctors Network accused the rebels of a drone attack on a displacement camp in Blue Nile state that killed 31 people, including four children.
Earlier this month, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova said that Sudanese troops recovered US-supplied weapons intended for Ukraine from RSF fighters near Bara. Their markings indicated that they had been transferred to Kiev in December 2024, she said, according to TASS.

articles.title: China Helped Russia Build a Shahed Drone Factory Producing Over 3,000 Attack Drones a Month

China Helped Russia Build a Shahed Drone Factory Producing Over 3,000 Attack Drones a Month
Russia’s Alabuga manufacturing complex has reportedly reached a production capacity of more than 3,000 gasoline-powered Shahed-type attack drones per month, supported by Chinese industrial equipment, engine components, batteries, and navigation technology.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on October 19, citing research by the US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Chinese companies supplied critical materials and manufacturing technology that helped Russia expand production of Geran-2 drones at its Alabuga facility in Tatarstan.
The report identifies several categories of Chinese assistance documented during 2024, including more than 685,000 components intended for Shahed drone engines, with an estimated combined value of $900,000. China also reportedly supplied 7,800 lithium-ion batteries used in the production process.
Beyond individual components, Chinese suppliers provided an industrial production line for manufacturing the airframes of long-range unmanned aerial vehicles. The equipment supported Russia’s efforts to establish domestic production capabilities rather than rely exclusively on imported, fully assembled drones.
The CSIS findings also indicate that Chinese authorities facilitated contacts between Russian defense contractors and Chinese industrial partners, helping establish supply relationships for the Alabuga production program.
Chinese technology reportedly contributed to the development of navigation systems designed to operate under electronic warfare conditions.
Russian engineers drew on research from the Beijing Institute of Microelectronics Technology while developing anti-jamming antennas for Shahed-type drones. Chinese manufacturer Harxon also supplied satellite navigation antennas that were reportedly classified as agricultural products during export.
Defense Express emphasized that the figures examined in the CSIS research cover documented Chinese deliveries during 2024. The limited reporting period does not establish whether similar assistance continued or stopped in 2023 or between 2025 and 2026.
The outlet reported that Alabuga’s current manufacturing capacity exceeds 3,000 gasoline-powered Shahed-type drones per month, alongside more than 3,500 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. The figures describe reported production capacity rather than independently verified monthly output.
China has also been linked to Russia’s ballistic missile production. In January 2026, reports revealed that Chinese precision machinery and dual-use technology were supporting the production of nuclear-capable Oreshnik missiles.

articles.title: Trump open to trilateral talks with Xi, Putin on denuclearization
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday he would consider holding three-way talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting nuclear disarmament could be a central focus of the meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," Trump told reporters outside the White House.
"If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it."
Trump indicated that nuclear disarmament would be a priority in any such meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," he said.
"We have more nuclear weapons than anybody. Russia is second, China is third, but catching up. China was way behind, and now they're catching up. It'll take about probably five years," Trump added.
Asked whether he would meet Putin and Xi to discuss ending the war without Zelenskyy present, Trump said he would do "anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not."
Earlier Monday, the Kremlin said that Putin, Trump and Xi could hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of next month's APEC summit in China and that a potential meeting had come up in talks.
Trump also renewed his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying "it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
"Maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate," Trump told reporters.
"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about. Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago," Trump told reporters before departing the White House.
"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine because what's happened? A tremendous number of people are dead. They're losing their male population," he said.
"Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing," he added.

articles.title: Putin suggests meeting with Trump, Xi to discuss Ukraine war resolution - report
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, the Wall Street Journal reported Sunday night, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The talks would not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, an unprecedented move which would be expected to alarm many European countries, WSJ wrote.
According to the report, the Kremlin suggested the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which takes place Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, southern China.
Putin first suggested the meeting while speaking to Trump on October 9, in the same conversation in which the two leaders agreed that the US would buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale, a former Russian intelligence officer told WSJ.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions over a potential meeting were ongoing.
“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told WSJ.
A senior US official told WSJ that Trump hadn't agreed to the meeting but may be receptive to the idea due to his desire to end the war.
Trump, Zelensky clash over Ukrainian attacks, US sanctions
This comes as Trump and Zelensky publicly criticize the other's decisions, with Zelensky saying on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, and Trump suggesting that Ukraine needs a new president.
Trump claimed that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," in a post on Truth Social earlier on Sunday, calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
Neither the White House nor the Chinese Embassy in Washington has commented on the report, but analysts told WSJ that a meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could advance Xi's ambitions for China's place in global diplomacy.
“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the US and Russia,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank, told WSJ.
However, Chinese officials have expressed concern that the meeting could overshadow China's role in the region at APEC, according to the report.
People familiar with the discussions told WSJ that Xi is also trying to balance support for Putin and economic ties with Europe. A meeting with Putin and Trump to discuss Ukraine could raise the risk of European backlash.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukrainian Sea Drones Could Extend US Army Strike Range Without Risking Crewed Vessels

Ukrainian Sea Drones Could Extend US Army Strike Range Without Risking Crewed Vessels
Ukraine’s Magura-type MV7 uncrewed surface vessels were tested as aerial drone carriers during a US Army exercise in Michigan, Defence Blog reported on October 18.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The vessels participated in Bayonet Quest 26, held from September 26 through October 6 by the 7th Infantry Division, part of Multi-Domain Command-Pacific. The division described the exercise as testing autonomous systems and uncrewed aircraft to extend sensing, operational reach, and decision-making.
Images and materials released by the division showed the Ukrainian-built vessels carrying dedicated platforms on their forward hulls, allowing aerial drones to launch directly from the boats. The exercise also paired autonomous maritime systems with a crewed Mk VI patrol boat.
The 7th Infantry Division did not disclose how many MV7 vessels participated, their exact configuration, or the type of aerial drones launched from them. Using an uncrewed boat as a drone carrier can extend aerial reconnaissance and strike range while keeping larger crewed vessels farther from potential threats.
Magura vessels became prominent through Ukrainian operations against Russia’s Black Sea Fleet near temporarily occupied Crimea. Ukraine later fielded variants equipped with missiles and machine guns, while Ukrainian military intelligence reported in 2025 that missile-armed Magura boats had downed Russian combat aircraft over the Black Sea.
The Michigan trials come as Ukrainian expertise in uncrewed maritime systems is increasingly built into allied exercises.
Days earlier, Ukraine used its DELTA battlefield management system to coordinate aerial, surface, and underwater drones with radar systems during NATO's REPMUS 2026 exercises, led by the Portuguese Navy.
It was Ukraine's third time taking part. Every system transmitting telemetry under NATO's STANAG 4817 standard was integrated into DELTA, which kept operating without interruption despite unstable communications.

articles.title: Fifteen months ago, Ukraine’s online arms store for front-line units didn’t exist. Now, it delivers 1 in 5 drones that state buys
articles.body:
Ukraine has turned buying weapons into something closer to online shopping. One in five drones bought by Ukraine's Defense Procurement Agency now reaches troops through DOT-Chain Defence, a state digital marketplace established in 2025 that lets combat units order what they need directly, the Defense Ministry says.
Drone technology changes so fast that a weapon ordered through months of paperwork can be obsolete before it arrives, so Ukraine built a marketplace that puts the choice in the hands of the units that fight. Launched in July 2025, DOT-Chain Defence now serves more than 500 combat units.
Unlike the agency’s other channels, central competitive tenders and fixed procurement lists, the marketplace lets commanders pick from a catalog themselves. The system works like an online store, where the military spends state funds to decide exactly what the state supplies them.
From a catalog to the trenches in eight days
Speed is the point of the model. When an item is in stock, the average time from a unit’s order to shipment is eight days, rising to about a month and a half for pre-orders, the ministry notes.
“Delivery speed is especially important for unmanned systems, because technology in this field develops dynamically,” DOT-Chain Defence chief Artem Romaniukov says.
Also, he states that makers and soldiers constantly rework designs to beat new countermeasures.
The catalog spans the main types of unmanned aerial vehicles, FPV drones, bombers and fixed-wing aircraft, along with their munitions, ground robotic systems and electronic-warfare gear.
Who carries the paperwork now
The shift moves the burden off the fighters. A unit builds its own order in DOT-Chain Defence, and the agency handles the procurement side, signing contracts with manufacturers and making payments. That means that purchases are completed in a few clicks.
In the first nine months of 2024, Ukraine’s troops received more than a million drones and other equipment through this system, part of a drone-buying surge that reached about $8 billion in the first half of the year.
